# Torque wrenches and bike torque values

## What a torque wrench is for

A torque wrench measures how hard a fastener is turned, in newton metres (Nm) or inch pounds (in lbf). Bolts on a bike are tightened to a specified torque so that the clamp force is right. Two things go wrong when the torque is off.

- Too loose: the part slips, rattles, or works free. A loose stem can rotate under braking. A loose crank can come off.
- Too tight: threads stretch or strip, aluminium parts deform, and carbon parts crack or crush. Carbon handlebars, seatposts, and frames are the most sensitive, because carbon fails suddenly rather than bending first.

A torque wrench lets you hit the specified number instead of guessing by feel. Click type wrenches give an audible click at the set value. Beam type show the value on a scale. Digital types show it on a screen. Use the wrench through its working range, usually the middle of its scale for best accuracy.

Rules that apply everywhere:

- Use the value printed on the component itself. Many carbon parts and stems print a maximum, and the number on the part overrides any general table.
- Clean and lightly lubricate threads only when the manufacturer says so. Grease changes the torque needed for the same clamp force. Dry threads and thread lock are often specified.
- Tighten in a cross pattern or in small steps when several bolts share a clamp, such as a stem or a rotor.
- Use a torque wrench for the final tightening only, and do not use it to loosen bolts.

## Common torque values

The ranges below are typical for many common components. They are a guide only. Always check the specification printed on the part or in the maker's manual, because values vary by brand and model.

### Cockpit

| Fastener | Typical value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Stem faceplate or steerer clamp bolts | 5 to 6 Nm | Holds the stem on the steerer. Too loose lets the bar twist. Too tight can crack carbon steerers. |
| Handlebar clamp bolts (stem to bar) | 5 to 6 Nm | Holds the bar. Carbon bars often have a stated maximum. Overtightening crushes them. |
| Brake lever clamp bolt | 4 to 6 Nm | Keeps the lever from rotating on the bar. |
| Shifter clamp bolt | 2 to 5 Nm | Holds the shifter in place. Low torque because the parts are small and thin. |
| Stem top cap bolt (headset preload) | Snug, then per the maker | Sets bearing preload. This is an adjustment, so follow the headset maker's method. |

### Seat and saddle

| Fastener | Typical value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Seatpost clamp bolt | 5 to 7 Nm | Holds the post in the frame. Too loose lets the saddle slip. Carbon posts may have a lower stated limit. |
| Saddle rail clamp bolts | 5 to 7 Nm | Holds the saddle on the post. Too tight can crack thin rails or the clamp. |

### Brakes

| Fastener | Typical value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Rim brake caliper mount bolt | 6 to 8 Nm | Holds the caliper so the pads stay aligned. |
| Disc brake caliper mount bolts | 6 to 8 Nm | Keeps the caliper square to the rotor. Some models go to 8 to 10 Nm. |
| Disc rotor bolts (6 bolt) | 2.5 to 4 Nm | Holds the rotor. Low torque because the bolts are small. |
| Centre lock rotor lockring | 40 to 50 Nm | Holds the rotor on a centre lock hub. Use the correct tool. |
| Hydraulic hose banjo bolt | 5 to 7 Nm | Seals the fluid line. Too tight can crack the fitting. Too loose can leak. |

### Drivetrain

| Fastener | Typical value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Crank arm bolt (Hollowtech or self-extracting) | 35 to 50 Nm | Holds the crank on the spindle. Under-torque can loosen the crank under pedal load. |
| Square taper crank bolt | 35 to 50 Nm | Holds the crank on the taper. Loose cranks wear the taper and the crank. |
| Pedals | 30 to 40 Nm | Holds the pedal in the crank. Right pedal tightens clockwise. Left pedal tightens counter-clockwise (reverse thread). |
| Bottom bracket cup (threaded) | 35 to 50 Nm | Holds the cups in the frame. Overtightening damages the threads in the shell. |
| Cassette lockring | 30 to 50 Nm | Holds the cassette on the hub. Loose cassettes click and wear quickly. |
| Chainring bolts | 8 to 12 Nm | Holds the rings to the crank. Uneven torque can bend the ring. |
| Front derailleur clamp bolt | 5 to 7 Nm | Holds the derailleur on the seat tube. Too loose lets it rotate. |
| Rear derailleur hanger bolt | 8 to 10 Nm | Holds the derailleur to the hanger. Loose derailleurs shift poorly. Check the hanger for damage. |

### Wheels

| Fastener | Typical value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Thru axle (front or rear) | 12 to 15 Nm | Clamps the wheel in the fork or frame. Loose axles can let the wheel come out. Check the axle maker's figure. |
| Quick release skewer | Not a torque setting | Set by lever force. The lever should leave a clear mark on your palm when closed. |

### Accessories

| Fastener | Typical value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Water bottle cage bolts | 4 to 5 Nm | Holds the cage. Overtightening cracks plastic and carbon bosses. |
| Rack and fender mounts | 5 to 6 Nm | Holds the accessory. Mounts on carbon frames often have stated limits. |

## Practical notes for a customer bike

- Start by looking for the printed torque limit on each carbon part. If the part does not show one, use the lower end of the range in this guide.
- Check the torque wrench is in calibration if it is used for many jobs.
- Record the torque values used on the work order, so the next mechanic knows the bike was set up to spec.

# Week-Long Bike Tour Packing Guide

Each item lists the reason it earns a place. Cut or swap items to fit your route, weather, and bike.

## Documents and money
- Passport or photo ID: needed for border crossings, hotel check-in, and emergencies.
- Paper copy of ID, insurance card, and emergency contacts: phones fail or die, and paper still works.
- Cash in local currency plus one backup card: some rural stops and campsites take cash only.
- Offline maps and the route file (GPX) saved to your phone: you need navigation with no signal.

## Bike repair kit
- Two tire levers: they pull a tire off the rim so you can fix a flat on the road.
- Spare inner tube sized to your wheels, plus a patch kit: punctures are the most common road failure.
- Mini pump or CO2 inflator: a flat you cannot inflate ends the ride.
- Multi-tool with chain breaker: covers most bolt adjustments and lets you repair a broken chain.
- Quick link matched to your chain: fixes a broken chain without a chain tool.
- Spoke wrench: loaded touring puts tension on spokes, and a loose spoke makes a wheel wobble.
- Tire boot (or a folded dollar bill or cardboard): covers a sidewall cut so the tube does not bulge through.
- Small bottle of chain lube: dust and rain wear a dry chain quickly.
- Rags or wet wipes: keep grease off your clothes and hands.
- Spare derailleur hanger, if your frame uses a bolt-on one: a bent hanger can end the tour, and a spare costs less than a lost day.

## Clothing
- Two cycling kits (bib shorts and jersey): wear one and wash the other each night.
- One warm mid layer: cold mornings and fast descents.
- Packable rain jacket: rain at speed feels colder than rain at a walk.
- Packable arm and leg warmers: they handle temperature swings through the day.
- Two casual outfits: you will want clothes that are not cycling shorts at dinner.
- Four cycling socks and two casual pairs: sweaty feet blister fast.
- Padded cycling gloves and a warm pair: padding protects palms if you fall, and warm gloves matter in cold mornings.
- Sun hat or buff, and sunglasses with a clear or light lens: the clear lens helps at dusk.
- Cycling shoes plus one light camp shoe or sandals: give your feet a break at night.

## Health and hygiene
- Sunscreen and lip balm with SPF: sun exposure on the bike is cumulative over days.
- Chamois cream: reduces saddle sores and chafing on long, repeated days.
- Pain reliever you normally use: muscle soreness builds through the week.
- Personal prescriptions in original bottles: keeps customs and pharmacies from asking questions.
- Blister kit (tape and moleskin): treats hot spots before they become open blisters.
- Electrolyte tablets: hot days drain sodium and fluids faster than you notice.
- Small first aid kit with antiseptic wipes: road rash gets infected without early cleaning.
- Travel toiletries and a quick-dry towel: campsites and budget hotels often lack good towels.

## Electronics and lights
- Phone charger and a power bank (10,000 mAh or more): navigation drains a phone in a few hours.
- Cables and a multi-port wall charger: you will charge several devices each night.
- Front and rear bike lights with spare batteries: cars must see you at dawn, dusk, and in tunnels.
- Bike computer or phone mount: keeps route and speed visible without stopping.

## Bags
- Pannier set or rear rack bag, waterproof: carries clothes and tools with the weight low and balanced.
- Handlebar bag or top tube bag: keeps snacks, phone, and sunscreen within reach.
- Dry bags for clothes and electronics: panniers leak in rain, and wet clothes stay wet for days.
- Small daypack for excursions off the bike: you carry it when you leave the bike behind.
- Luggage locks: deter opportunistic theft at hostels and train stations.

## Food and water
- Two water bottles at minimum: one bottle runs dry on climbs and in heat.
- Snacks such as bars, nuts, or dried fruit: keep energy up between meals. Long riding can burn several hundred calories per hour, so eat before you feel hungry.
- Reusable cup and spork: useful at cafes, markets, and campsites.

## Flying with the bike
- Bike box or hard case: the airline may refuse a bike in a soft bag, and a box protects the frame.
- Remove pedals, turn the handlebars parallel to the frame, and deflate tires to about half pressure: this reduces damage and fits the box.
- Pedal wrench and Allen keys for reassembly: you need them at the destination.
- Packing tape and zip ties: secure loose parts and the box.
- Check the airline bike fee, size limit, and box rules before you travel: fees and rules vary by carrier.

## Before you leave
- Test-ride the loaded bike for at least an hour: load changes handling and braking.
- Check brake pads and cables, and confirm tires hold pressure: this prevents a breakdown on day one.
- Practice a tire change on the actual wheels: doing it on the road for the first time costs time.

- Bike computer or phone mount: keeps route and speed visible without stopping.

## Bags
- Pannier set or rear rack bag, waterproof: carries clothes and tools with the weight low and balanced.
- Handlebar bag or top tube bag: keeps snacks, phone, and sunscreen within reach.
- Dry bags for clothes and electronics: panniers leak in rain, and wet clothes stay wet for days.
- Small daypack for excursions off the bike: you carry it when you leave the bike behind.
- Luggage locks: deter opportunistic theft at hostels and train stations.

## Food and water
- Two water bottles at minimum: one bottle runs dry on climbs and in heat.
- Snacks such as bars, nuts, or dried fruit: keep energy up between meals. Long riding can burn several hundred calories per hour, so eat before you feel hungry.
- Reusable cup and spork: useful at cafes, markets, and campsites.

## Flying with the bike
- Bike box or hard case: the airline may refuse a bike in a soft bag, and a box protects the frame.
- Remove pedals, turn the handlebars parallel to the frame, and deflate tires to about half pressure: this reduces damage and fits the box.

- Packing tape and zip ties: secure loose parts and the box.
- Check the airline bike fee, size limit, and box rules before you travel: fees and rules vary by carrier.

- Test-ride the loaded bike for at least an hour: load changes handling and braking.
- Check brake pads and cables, and confirm tires hold pressure: this prevents a breakdown on day one.
- Practice a tire change on the actual wheels: doing it on the road for the first time costs time.

# Week-Long Bike Tour Packing Guide

Assumptions: self-supported touring on a loaded touring or gravel bike, 5 to 7 days, mixed weather, overnights in hotels, campsites, or hosts. Adjust quantities if your trip differs.

## Carry on the plane

Bike parts and tools often cannot go in carry-on luggage, but these should stay with you:

- Passport, tickets, and a printed copy of your booking and tour route. Reason: airlines and borders need them, and paper survives a dead phone.
- Offline maps. Download the route and region in your map app before you leave. Reason: you will have no signal on the plane or in remote areas.
- Charged power bank and cables. Reason: phones drain fast on maps and cameras, and airport outlets are scarce.
- Multi-tool or pedal wrench only if your airline allows it. Reason: many carriers ban tools in carry-on, so check first.

## Bike and bike tools

- Bike box or soft case, packed by you or the shop. Reason: a poorly packed bike gets damaged in transit.
- Pedals removed and stored in a bag, handlebar turned, wheels removed or protected. Reason: these are the most common damage points and make reassembly faster.
- Tire levers (2 to 3). Reason: they pry tires off rims for flat repairs.
- Spare tubes (2 to 3, matching your tire size). Reason: one flat per day is common on long tours.
- Patch kit and spare tire boot. Reason: patches fix small holes, and a boot covers a tire cut.
- Mini pump or CO2 inflator with spare cartridges. Reason: you need a way to inflate after a flat.
- Multi-tool with chain breaker and hex keys. Reason: it covers most adjustments and chain repairs.
- Spare quick link or chain master link matched to your chain. Reason: a broken chain stops the tour without one.
- Spoke wrench and a few spare spokes if your wheels are built for touring. Reason: broken spokes are common on loaded wheels.
- Chain lube and a rag. Reason: a dry chain wears fast and squeaks.
- Brake pads, spare derailleur hanger, and cable ties. Reason: these fix common breakdowns that stop a rider.
- Pannier or frame bag and mounts checked before the trip. Reason: a loose rack or bag can break on the road.

## Clothing

Pack for layers. Plan for about 4 to 5 cycling kits so you can rinse one each day.

- 4 to 5 cycling jerseys and shorts. Reason: padded shorts reduce saddle soreness over long days.
- 2 pairs of cycling socks. Reason: wool or synthetic socks dry quickly after washing.
- Thin base layer top. Reason: it manages sweat on cool mornings.
- Warm mid layer or fleece. Reason: temperatures drop after sunset, especially at altitude or near water.
- Waterproof rain jacket and rain pants. Reason: rain on a bike is cold and sustained.
- Lightweight wind vest. Reason: it blocks wind on descents without much bulk.
- Cycling gloves. Reason: they protect hands in a fall and reduce numbness.
- Warm hat or buff, and sun cap. Reason: heat loss and sun exposure both matter on a tour.
- Casual clothes for evenings: 1 pair of pants or shorts, 2 shirts. Reason: cycling kit is not suitable for indoor dinners.
- Sleepwear and underwear for 6 to 7 days. Reason: clean dry clothes at night help recovery.
- Sandals or light shoes. Reason: they give your feet a break from cycling shoes.

## Shoes

- Cycling shoes. Reason: the shoes you ride in are the ones that matter most for comfort.
- Pedals matched to your shoes. Reason: clip pedals need matching cleats, so check before you leave.

## Sleep and camping (only if you are camping)

- Tent or hammock, with stakes and a footprint. Reason: a ground sheet protects the tent floor.
- Sleeping bag rated for the coldest night you expect. Reason: cold nights cause poor sleep and slow recovery.
- Sleeping pad. Reason: it insulates you from the ground and gives comfort.
- Headlamp with spare batteries. Reason: you need light for camp chores and bike repairs after dark.

## Toiletries and health

- Sunscreen, lip balm, and insect repellent. Reason: long days in the sun and wildlife both cause problems.
- Chamois cream. Reason: it prevents chafing on long rides.
- Personal medications in original containers, plus a copy of prescriptions. Reason: you may not find them on the road.
- First aid kit: bandages, antiseptic, blister pads, pain relief, and an electrolyte mix. Reason: road rash and blisters are the most common injuries on tours.
- Basic toiletries in small bottles. Reason: they are light and cover daily needs.
- Microfiber towel. Reason: it dries quickly and packs small.

## Electronics

- Phone, charger, and a cable. Reason: you need navigation and emergency contact.
- Bike computer or phone mount. Reason: it shows route and speed.
- Power bank (at least 10,000 mAh). Reason: it recharges your phone and light between stops.
- Bike light set (front and rear) with spare batteries. Reason: lights are required for riding in dusk or tunnels.
- Camera if you want one. Reason: it keeps photos separate from your phone battery.

## Navigation and documents

- Printed route map and cue sheet. Reason: you need a backup if your phone fails.
- Cash in local currency and a card. Reason: rural areas often lack card readers.
- Travel insurance details and emergency contacts. Reason: you need them if you get hurt or the bike is damaged.
- Helmet and eyewear. Reason: head protection is the most important safety item on the road.

## Packing system

- Panniers or a rear rack bag: keep clothes dry in waterproof stuff sacks.
- Front bag or handlebar bag: keep snacks, phone, and tools reachable.
- Frame bag: holds tools and spare tubes.
- Pack heavy items low and centered to keep the bike stable.

## Before you leave

- Ride the loaded bike for at least one day. Reason: you find rubbing, loose racks, and saddle problems early.
- Check all bolts and brake pads. Reason: loaded bikes loosen over time.
- Test your tools and check your spare parts list against your bike.

## Final checklist

- [ ] Bike packed and protected
- [ ] Tools and spare tubes packed
- [ ] Clothes packed in waterproof bags
- [ ] Electronics and power bank charged
- [ ] Passport, tickets, and route printed
- [ ] Offline maps downloaded

# Winter Storage Routine

**Cleaning.** Wash the bike before storing it, because road salt, grit, and wet mud corrode chains and bearings over winter. Use a bucket of warm water with mild soap and a soft brush, then rinse with a garden hose on low pressure. Keep water away from the bottom bracket, headset, and hub seals. Degrease the chain and drivetrain, rinse, and dry every part with a clean rag before moving on.

**Lubrication.** Once the drivetrain is dry, apply a fresh coat of chain lube and turn the pedals backward so the lube works into every link. Wipe off the excess with a clean rag, since extra lube attracts dirt. Put a light oil on the derailleur pivots, brake pivots, and cable housings. Grease the seatpost, pedal threads, and any exposed bolts to prevent seizing. Check the headset and bottom bracket for play, and regrease them if needed.

**Tires.** Inflate the tires to about half of the maximum pressure printed on the sidewall. This keeps the tires from sagging and slows sidewall cracking. Check the sidewalls for cracks or bulges, and note any damaged tire for replacement in spring. If the bike will sit for months, lift it off the floor or hang it so no single tire carries its weight for a long time. Before the first spring ride, top the tires up to the full pressure printed on the sidewall.

**Where to keep the bike.** Store the bike indoors in a cool, dry space with good airflow and away from direct sun. Avoid unheated sheds and damp basements, because moisture and temperature swings cause rust and rubber damage. Hang the bike by its frame or set it on a stand so the tires do not bear its weight. Cover it loosely with a breathable cloth rather than plastic, which traps condensation. Keep the bike away from furnaces, fuel, and fertilizers.

# Brake Check Procedure for New Volunteers

Fern Hollow Bicycle Cooperative

Run this check on every bike before it goes back to a member. Do the rim brake or disc brake section that matches the bike. If a bike has both kinds of wheel, check both.

If any step fails, tag the bike, set it aside, and tell the shop lead. Do not return a bike with a failed check to a member.

## Part 1: Rim Brakes

Tools: 4 mm and 5 mm Allen keys, a ruler, a clean rag, isopropyl alcohol.

1. Inspect the pads.
   - Pad rubber is clean and free of grit, oil, and glaze.
   - Pad rubber is not worn past the wear groove or indicator line.
   - Pads are not cracked, hardened, or separating from the holder.
2. Check pad alignment.
   - The pad hits the braking surface of the rim, not the tire or a spoke.
   - Toe in is set. The front edge of each pad should touch the rim about 1 mm before the rear edge.
3. Check centering.
   - Both pads sit the same distance from the rim.
   - Adjust with the centering screw on the caliper if needed.
4. Squeeze the brake lever firmly.
   - Both pads close on the rim at the same time.
   - The lever stops well short of the handlebar when fully squeezed.
   - The brake does not feel spongy, and the lever does not pull to one side.
5. Check the cable.
   - The cable slides freely through the housing.
   - No frayed or kinked cable, and no cracked housing ends.
   - The cable pinch bolt is tight.
6. Check the caliper.
   - Caliper mount bolts are tight, and the caliper does not rock.
   - Brake arms return smoothly after release.
7. Check the rim braking surface.
   - The rim walls have no grooves deeper than the wear indicator, no bulges, and no cracks.
   - If the wear indicator is gone, or the rim is cracked or bulged, fail the bike.
8. Spin the wheel.
   - The wheel turns without rubbing the pads.
   - The rim runs true near the brake track.
9. Confirm the wheel is secure.
   - Quick release is closed with the lever facing the correct way, or the thru axle is fully seated.
   - Pull the wheel side to side. It should not move.
10. Final stop test.
    - Squeeze hard and roll the bike forward. It should stop without slipping or squealing.

## Part 2: Disc Brakes

Tools: T25 Torx key, 4 mm and 5 mm Allen keys, isopropyl alcohol, clean rag, ruler.

Do not put oil, grease, or any lubricant on the rotor or pads. Clean the rotor with isopropyl alcohol only.

1. Inspect the rotor.
   - The rotor is free of oil, dirt, and brake fluid.
   - No cracks, no warping, and no blue or scorched spots.
   - Thickness is above the minimum stamped on the rotor. If you cannot find a minimum, ask the lead.
2. Check rotor bolts.
   - All rotor bolts are tight. Use the torque printed on the part or in the manufacturer manual.
   - Check the rotor for a bend by spinning the wheel and watching the gap between the rotor and the pads. The rotor should not rub.
3. Inspect the pads.
   - Friction material is above the wear indicator, or at least about 0.5 mm thick.
   - Pads are not glazed, contaminated, or cracked.
   - Pad retaining clip or pin is in place.
4. Check the caliper.
   - Caliper mount bolts are tight, and the caliper does not rock.
   - Caliper is centered over the rotor. If it is not, loosen the mount bolts, squeeze the lever to center the pads, hold the lever, and tighten the bolts.
5. Check the hydraulic system (hydraulic brakes only).
   - The lever feels firm, not spongy, when squeezed.
   - Fluid level in the reservoir is between the min and max marks.
   - No fluid is leaking from the hose fittings, the caliper, or the lever.
   - Do not open a hydraulic system or bleed brakes unless a lead has trained you.
6. Check the cable (mechanical brakes only).
   - Cable slides freely, is not frayed, and the pinch bolt is tight.
   - Pads are adjusted to the rotor with equal clearance on both sides.
7. Spin the wheel.
   - No rubbing or ticking from the pads.
8. Confirm the wheel is secure.
   - Quick release is closed with the lever facing the correct way, or the thru axle is fully seated.
   - Pull the wheel side to side. It should not move.
9. Final stop test.
   - Squeeze the lever. It should feel firm, and the wheel should lock or slow strongly.
   - Roll the bike forward and stop. There should be no squeal, grinding, or pulsing.

## After the Check

- Write the bike tag with the date, your name, and PASS or FAIL.
- On FAIL, tag the bike with the failing step and tell the shop lead before doing anything else.
- Do not fix brake problems you are not sure about. Ask the lead.

# Fern Hollow Bicycle Cooperative: Brake Check Procedure for New Volunteers

Use this sheet for every bike that comes through the shop for a brake check. Read the section for the brake type on the bike. Some bikes have both a front and rear brake of different types, so check each brake on its own.

If you find any fault you are not sure how to fix, tag the bike as "Do not ride" and tell the shift lead. Never ride a bike with a brake you have doubts about.

## Before you start (both brake types)

1. Lift the front wheel and spin it by hand. It should spin freely and stop gradually. Watch for rubbing and wobble.
2. Repeat for the rear wheel.
3. Check that the quick release levers or thru axles are closed and tight. The wheel should not move side to side in the dropouts.
4. Squeeze each brake lever firmly. Note whether the lever stops well before it touches the handlebar.

## Rim brakes (caliper, cantilever, and V brakes)

Rim brakes squeeze pads against the metal sides of the wheel rim.

1. **Pad contact.** Squeeze the lever and look at each pad. The pad should land on the rim's braking surface, not on the tire, the spokes, or the rim edge.
2. **Pad toe in.** The front edge of each pad should touch the rim about 1 mm before the back edge. This makes the pad squeal less and wear evenly.
3. **Pad wear.** Replace the pads if the wear indicator groove is gone, if the rubber is cracked or hard, or if the pad is contaminated with oil or grease.
4. **Pad cleaning.** If a pad is glazed or dirty but not worn out, clean the pad and rim braking surface with isopropyl alcohol. Let them dry before riding.
5. **Rim condition.** Look at the brake track on the rim. Replace the rim or tag the wheel if you see deep grooves, a bulge or bubble on the sidewall, a crack, or a worn spot that makes the rim thin.
6. **Centering.** Squeeze the lever. Both pads should reach the rim at the same time. If one pad hits first, adjust the centering screw until both touch together.
7. **Lever stop.** The lever should not touch the handlebar when fully squeezed. If it does, tighten the cable or replace the brake pad so it reaches the rim sooner.
8. **Cable and housing.** Check the cable for fraying, kinks, or rust. Check that the housing ends are not split and that the cable anchor bolt is tight.
9. **Brake stop.** Squeeze the lever hard. The wheel should stop within a short distance. A spongy or slow stop means a fault. Tag the bike.
10. **Final spin test.** Spin the wheel again. It should spin freely with no pad rubbing.

## Disc brakes (mechanical or hydraulic)

Disc brakes squeeze pads against a rotor attached to the hub.

1. **Rotor condition.** Look at the rotor surface. Replace it if you see cracks, a bent or warped shape, or a surface that is heavily scored. Check the thickness marking on the rotor if one is printed. Replace it when it is at or below the minimum.
2. **Rotor bolts.** Check that all rotor bolts are tight. Use a torque wrench at the value on the rotor or the tool manual.
3. **Rotor cleanliness.** Keep oil and grease off the rotor. If it is contaminated, clean it with isopropyl alcohol on a clean cloth. Do not touch the braking surface with bare hands.
4. **Pad wear.** Look at the pad material. Replace the pads when the material is near the backing plate, usually about 1 mm left. Also replace them if they are glazed, cracked, or contaminated.
5. **Caliper alignment.** Spin the wheel and check that the rotor passes between the pads without rubbing. If the rotor rubs, loosen the caliper mounting bolts, squeeze the lever to center the caliper, and hold the lever while you tighten the bolts.
6. **Lever feel (hydraulic).** Squeeze the lever. It should feel firm and stop the wheel. A spongy or soft lever means air in the system or a leak. Tag the bike and tell the shift lead. Do not bleed a hydraulic brake unless you have been trained to do it.
7. **Lever feel (mechanical).** Squeeze the lever. Check the cable tension and adjust it at the barrel adjuster or the caliper if the lever travels too far.
8. **Fluid and leaks (hydraulic).** Check the hoses, fittings, and caliper for oil or fluid leaks. Check the reservoir fluid level. Do not mix fluid types. If a leak is present, tag the bike.
9. **Cable and housing (mechanical).** Check for fraying, kinks, or rust. Check the housing ends and cable anchor bolt.
10. **Lever stop.** The lever should not touch the handlebar when fully squeezed.
11. **Brake stop.** Squeeze the lever hard. The wheel should stop within a short distance with no grinding or pulsing.
12. **Final spin test.** Spin the wheel. It should spin freely with no rubbing or squeal.

## When to tag the bike "Do not ride"

- A rotor or rim is cracked, bent, or worn past its limit.
- Pads are worn to the minimum or contaminated and you cannot clean them.
- The lever is spongy or the brake does not stop the wheel.
- You see fluid leaks or a damaged housing or cable.
- Any fault you are not sure how to fix.

Always tell the shift lead before you release a bike that was tagged.

# Torque Wrench Guide for Bicycles

## What a torque wrench is for

A torque wrench measures the rotational force applied to a fastener and lets you stop at a set value. Bicycle fasteners are small, and many parts are aluminum or carbon fiber. Tightening by feel causes two kinds of failure:

- Overtightening. Threads strip, aluminum parts crack, and carbon parts can crack or crush. A cracked carbon seatpost, handlebar, or stem can fail under load and cause a crash.
- Undertightening. Bolts loosen during riding. A stem can rotate, a seatpost can slip, a brake caliper can shift, or a crank can work loose.

A torque wrench removes guesswork. It matters most on carbon components, small bolts, and any part with a torque value printed on it.

## How to use one

1. Set the wrench to the value in the component marking or the manufacturer manual. Turn the wrench back to its lowest setting when you store it, so the spring stays relaxed.
2. Use the correct bit or socket. A worn bit can slip and round the bolt head.
3. Pull smoothly until the wrench clicks or the display signals. Stop at the click. Do not keep pulling.
4. Check whether the threads are dry or lubricated. Grease or anti-seize changes the torque a bolt reaches for the same clamp force. Use the value that matches the thread condition in the manual.
5. Tighten in a cross pattern on multi-bolt parts, such as caliper and rotor bolts.

If a manufacturer gives a range, use the middle of the range. If a part has no marking, a conservative value from the list below is a reasonable starting point, but check manufacturer documentation when you can.

## Common torque values across a bike

Values are typical. Always use the number printed on the component when one exists. Values are in newton meters (Nm).

### Cockpit (handlebar and stem)

- Stem faceplate bolts (threadless steerer): 5 Nm, range 4 to 6. Reason: clamps the steerer. Too loose lets the stem rotate or slip. Too tight can crack the steerer or the stem.
- Handlebar clamp bolts: 5 Nm, range 4 to 6. Reason: holds the bar in place. Carbon bars often print a maximum, so check the bar.
- Seatpost clamp bolt: 5 to 6 Nm. Reason: holds the post. Carbon posts are especially sensitive to overtightening.
- Saddle rail clamp: 4 to 5 Nm. Reason: holds the saddle. Too tight can crack rails.
- Hydraulic brake lever clamp: about 5 Nm. Reason: holds the lever. Too loose lets the lever rotate under braking.
- Shifter clamp: 2 to 5 Nm. Reason: holds the shifter. Check the manual for carbon bars.

### Brakes

- Caliper mounting bolts (road and post mount): 6 to 8 Nm. Reason: holds the caliper square to the rotor. Loose bolts cause rubbing or noise.
- Six bolt rotor bolts: 2.5 to 4 Nm. Reason: holds the rotor. Overtightening can warp or crack the rotor. Undertightening lets the rotor wobble.
- Center lock lockring: about 40 Nm, check the hub. Reason: holds the rotor on the hub. Use the specific lockring tool.

### Wheels

- Front thru axle (15 mm): about 8 to 10 Nm. Reason: holds the wheel in the fork. Check the hub and fork value.
- Rear thru axle: about 12 to 15 Nm. Reason: holds the wheel in the frame. Check the hub value.
- Quick release: no torque value. Set by hand to clamp force. Close the lever firmly and check the lever position.

### Drivetrain

- Crank bolt (Hollowtech or square taper): 35 to 50 Nm. Reason: holds the crank on the spindle. A loose crank can damage the spindle and the crank.
- Pedals (15 mm thread): about 35 Nm. Reason: pedals loosen with pedaling. Grease the threads and tighten both pedals.
- Bottom bracket cups: 35 to 50 Nm. Reason: holds the bearing cups. Check the frame and cup value.
- Chainring bolts: 8 to 12 Nm. Reason: holds rings on the crank arm. Tighten evenly across all bolts.
- Cassette lockring: 30 to 50 Nm, often about 40 Nm. Reason: holds the cassette on the freehub. A loose cassette clicks and can damage the freehub.
- Rear derailleur mounting bolt: about 8 to 10 Nm. Reason: holds the derailleur on the hanger. Check the value on the derailleur.
- Derailleur hanger bolt: about 4 to 6 Nm. Reason: holds the hanger. Check the frame manual.

### Frame and accessories

- Water bottle cage bolts: about 4 to 5 Nm. Reason: holds the cage. Carbon frames often have a lower limit, so check the frame.
- Fender and rack bolts: about 4 to 6 Nm. Reason: holds the accessory. Use the lowest value that keeps it steady.

## Notes

- These values are common published ranges for typical components. They are not a substitute for the manufacturer documentation for the specific part.
- Carbon parts need the most care. Use a torque wrench and the exact value from the manufacturer.
- Thread lubricant changes the result. Follow the manual for dry or lubricated threads.
- A torque wrench is a precision tool. Check its calibration periodically, and store it at its lowest setting.

A torque wrench measures the rotational force applied to a fastener and lets you stop at a set value. Bicycle fasteners are small, and many parts are aluminum or carbon fiber. Tightening by feel causes two kinds of failure:

- Overtightening. Threads strip, aluminum parts crack, and carbon parts can crack or crush. A cracked carbon seatpost, handlebar, or stem can fail under load and cause a crash.
- Undertightening. Bolts loosen during riding. A stem can rotate, a seatpost can slip, a brake caliper can shift, or a crank can work loose.

A torque wrench removes guesswork. It matters most on carbon components, small bolts, and any part with a torque value printed on it.

## How to use one

1. Set the wrench to the value in the component marking or the manufacturer manual. Turn the wrench back to its lowest setting when you store it, so the spring stays relaxed.
2. Use the correct bit or socket. A worn bit can slip and round the bolt head.
3. Pull smoothly until the wrench clicks or the display signals. Stop at the click. Do not keep pulling.
4. Check whether the threads are dry or lubricated. Grease or anti-seize changes the torque a bolt reaches for the same clamp force. Use the value that matches the thread condition in the manual.
5. Tighten in a cross pattern on multi-bolt parts, such as caliper and rotor bolts.

If a manufacturer gives a range, use the middle of the range. If a part has no marking, a conservative value from the list below is a reasonable starting point, but check manufacturer documentation when you can.

## Common torque values across a bike

Values are typical. Always use the number printed on the component when one exists. Values are in newton meters (Nm).

### Cockpit (handlebar and stem)

- Stem faceplate bolts (threadless steerer): 5 Nm, range 4 to 6. Reason: clamps the steerer. Too loose lets the stem rotate or slip. Too tight can crack the steerer or the stem.
- Handlebar clamp bolts: 5 Nm, range 4 to 6. Reason: holds the bar in place. Carbon bars often print a maximum, so check the bar.
- Seatpost clamp bolt: 5 to 6 Nm. Reason: holds the post. Carbon posts are especially sensitive to overtightening.
- Saddle rail clamp: 4 to 5 Nm. Reason: holds the saddle. Too tight can crack rails.
- Hydraulic brake lever clamp: about 5 Nm. Reason: holds the lever. Too loose lets the lever rotate under braking.
- Shifter clamp: 2 to 5 Nm. Reason: holds the shifter. Check the manual for carbon bars.

### Brakes

- Caliper mounting bolts (road and post mount): 6 to 8 Nm. Reason: holds the caliper square to the rotor. Loose bolts cause rubbing or noise.
- Six bolt rotor bolts: 2.5 to 4 Nm. Reason: holds the rotor. Overtightening can warp or crack the rotor. Undertightening lets the rotor wobble.
- Center lock lockring: about 40 Nm, check the hub. Reason: holds the rotor on the hub. Use the specific lockring tool.

### Wheels

- Front thru axle (15 mm): about 8 to 10 Nm. Reason: holds the wheel in the fork. Check the hub and fork value.
- Rear thru axle: about 12 to 15 Nm. Reason: holds the wheel in the frame. Check the hub value.
- Quick release: no torque value. Set by hand to clamp force. Close the lever firmly and check the lever position.

### Drivetrain

- Crank bolt (Hollowtech or square taper): 35 to 50 Nm. Reason: holds the crank on the spindle. A loose crank can damage the spindle and the crank.
- Pedals (15 mm thread): about 35 Nm. Reason: pedals loosen with pedaling. Grease the threads and tighten both pedals.
- Bottom bracket cups: 35 to 50 Nm. Reason: holds the bearing cups. Check the frame and cup value.
- Chainring bolts: 8 to 12 Nm. Reason: holds rings on the crank arm. Tighten evenly across all bolts.
- Cassette lockring: 30 to 50 Nm, often about 40 Nm. Reason: holds the cassette on the freehub. A loose cassette clicks and can damage the freehub.
- Rear derailleur mounting bolt: about 8 to 10 Nm. Reason: holds the derailleur on the hanger. Check the value on the derailleur.
- Derailleur hanger bolt: about 4 to 6 Nm. Reason: holds the hanger. Check the frame manual.

### Frame and accessories

- Water bottle cage bolts: about 4 to 5 Nm. Reason: holds the cage. Carbon frames often have a lower limit, so check the frame.
- Fender and rack bolts: about 4 to 6 Nm. Reason: holds the accessory. Use the lowest value that keeps it steady.

## Notes

- These values are common published ranges for typical components. They are not a substitute for the manufacturer documentation for the specific part.
- Carbon parts need the most care. Use a torque wrench and the exact value from the manufacturer.
- Thread lubricant changes the result. Follow the manual for dry or lubricated threads.
- A torque wrench is a precision tool. Check its calibration periodically, and store it at its lowest setting.

# Chain and cassette wear

## Why chains wear out

A bicycle chain is a row of small steel pins and rollers. Each link pivots thousands of times per ride. Every pivot rubs metal on metal, and grit from the road gets pressed into that rubbing surface. Over time the pins and the inner plates wear slightly, and the gap between each pair of pins grows. The chain gets longer. It does not stretch in the sense of the metal bending. The pitch simply opens up.

Three things speed up this wear:

1. Dirt and grit. Sand acts like grinding paste inside the joints.
2. Dry or old lube. Without a film of lube, the pins rub directly on each other.
3. Riding in wet or salty conditions, which washes lube out and lets rust form.

A worn chain also wears the cassette and chainrings faster, because the stretched chain no longer seats cleanly on the teeth.

## How to measure chain wear

Use a chain wear gauge, or a steel ruler.

1. Clean the chain so grit does not hide the true length.
2. Hook the gauge pin into a roller and let the gauge hang straight.
3. Read the marking. Many gauges read 0.5 and 0.75 directly as percent elongation.

Without a gauge, measure the length:

1. Pull the chain taut.
2. Measure from the center of one roller pin to the center of the pin 12 links away. A new chain measures 12.00 inches.
3. Compare the reading to the table below.

| Measured length (12 links) | Wear | Action |
|---|---|---|
| 12.00 to 12.06 in | Under 0.5 percent | Chain is fine |
| 12.06 to 12.09 in | 0.5 to 0.75 percent | Plan a replacement |
| 12.09 in or more | Over 0.75 percent | Replace the chain now |

The 0.75 percent point is the usual limit. Past it, the chain starts to ride up on the cassette teeth and can skip under load.

## When to replace the chain

Replace the chain when it reads 0.75 percent. Also replace it when:

- It skips under pedaling, even at 0.75 percent or less. A dirty or damaged link can cause this too.
- It binds or stiffens at one link, which often means a bent pin or a rusted joint.
- A link is cracked or a pin has come loose.

Replacing a chain is cheap compared with replacing a cassette and chainrings. Do it on time.

## Why cassettes wear out

The cassette is the set of rear sprockets. Each tooth is in contact with the chain for a short time on every pedal stroke. Over many miles the chain rollers wear the tooth faces. The teeth take on a hooked or shark fin shape. A new chain on a worn cassette will then skip, because the roller cannot settle into the groove.

## How to measure cassette wear

The cassette has no simple gauge. Check it by looking and feeling:

1. Look at the teeth on the cog used most, often the largest or the one you ride in most. A worn tooth looks pointed or hooked, like a shark fin.
2. Pull the chain away from the cassette at the rear. If the teeth lift with it, the cassette is worn.
3. Shift through the cogs while pedaling. Skipping or jumping under load points to a worn cassette, a worn chain, or both.

## When to replace the cassette

Replace the cassette when:

- The teeth on the most used cogs look hooked or pointed.
- The chain skips on the cassette even after you install a new chain.
- The chain lifts off the teeth when pulled away.

A common rule: replace the chain at 0.75 percent. If the chain has run past 0.75 percent for a long time, expect the cassette to be worn too. Replace the chain and cassette together in that case. Installing a new chain on a worn cassette wastes the new chain.

## Practical checklist

- Measure the chain every few hundred miles or each month of regular riding.
- Clean and lube the chain after wet rides.
- Log the date and reading so you can see the wear rate.
- Check the cassette for shark fin teeth each time you replace the chain.

The full step-by-step guide is in workbench/roadside-tube-patch-guide.md. Here are the core steps:

1. Shift to the smallest rear cog, then remove the wheel.
2. Let out the air. Push the tire bead into the rim's center.
3. Hook a tire lever under the bead by the valve, hook it to a spoke, and pry with a second lever a hand's width away.
4. Pull the tube out, valve first.
5. Find the hole by listening, feeling, or dipping in water. Check the tire for the cause.
6. Rough the area around the hole, apply thin glue, wait until tacky, and press the patch on for 30 seconds.
7. Insert a lightly inflated tube, seat the tire, then inflate to the sidewall pressure.
8. Reinstall the wheel and check that it spins without rubbing.

# Roadside Tube Patch Guide

You need: tire levers (2 or 3), a patch kit with glue or self-adhesive patches, sandpaper or the rough scraper in the kit, a pump or spare tube, and a bowl of water if you have one.

## 1. Remove the wheel
1. Shift the chain to the smallest rear cog so the wheel slides out easily.
2. Rear wheel: open the quick release lever or loosen the axle nuts. Lift the chain off the small cog, then pull the wheel out of the dropouts.
3. Front wheel: open the quick release or loosen the nuts, then lift the wheel out.

## 2. Deflate and remove the tire
1. Press the valve core to let out any remaining air.
2. Push the tire bead (the edge) away from the rim on both sides, all the way around, into the center of the rim.
3. Hook one tire lever under the bead next to the valve. Hook it onto a spoke so it stays put.
4. Insert a second lever a hand's width away and pry the bead over the rim. Repeat with a third lever if needed.
5. Pull the tube out of the tire, starting at the valve. Keep the valve in hand so it does not slip back in.

## 3. Find the hole
1. Pump the tube slightly so it holds shape.
2. Find the hole by one of these methods:
   - Listen and feel for escaping air.
   - Run the tube past your cheek or lips.
   - Dip sections in water and watch for bubbles.
3. Look at the tire too. Run your fingers slowly around the inside to find the cause, such as a thorn, glass, or a wire puncture. Remove anything you find, or the new tube will fail the same way.
4. Mark the hole with a pen or chalk.

## 4. Prepare the patch area
1. Dry the area around the hole.
2. Rough the area with sandpaper or the scraper in the kit, about 3 cm around the hole. Do not touch the roughed surface with your fingers.
3. Wipe away the dust.

## 5. Apply glue and patch (if using glue)
1. Spread a thin layer of glue over the roughed area. Go a bit larger than the patch.
2. Wait until the glue is tacky, about 1 to 3 minutes. It should feel sticky but not wet.
3. Peel the foil from the patch without touching the adhesive side.
4. Press the patch firmly onto the hole. Hold for 30 seconds or more.

## 5b. Self-adhesive patch
1. Clean and rough the area as above.
2. Peel the backing and press the patch on. Hold firmly for 30 seconds.

## 6. Check the tire
1. Make sure the tire has no sharp objects left inside.
2. If you found a cut in the tire, place a folded piece of tire boot or a dollar bill inside the tire over the cut so the tube cannot bulge through.

## 7. Install the tube
1. Put a little air in the tube so it takes shape, but keep it soft.
2. Insert the valve into the valve hole in the rim first.
3. Tuck the tube evenly into the tire, starting at the valve and working around. Make sure the tube is not pinched between the bead and rim.
4. Check that the tube sits evenly all the way around.

## 8. Reseat the tire
1. Push the tire bead back onto the rim, starting at the valve. Work with your thumbs.
2. Finish the last section by hand. Use a lever only as a last resort, and watch that you do not pinch the tube.
3. Check that the valve sits straight and the tube is not visible between the tire and rim.

## 9. Inflate
1. Pump to the pressure printed on the tire sidewall, or firm but not rock hard if unsure.
2. Spin the wheel and watch that it runs true and the tire is even.

## 10. Reinstall the wheel
1. Put the wheel back into the frame and seat it fully in the dropouts.
2. Rear wheel: place the chain on the smallest cog, then tighten the quick release or nuts.
3. Front wheel: tighten the quick release or nuts.
4. Squeeze the brakes and spin the wheel to check it does not rub.

## Tips
- If the valve is a presta valve, unscrew the lock nut before pumping, and keep the valve tip straight.
- Check the tire again after a few kilometers to make sure it holds air.

# Chain and Cassette Wear

## Why chains wear out

A bike chain is a row of metal links. Each link has two plates held by pins, and each pin sits inside a roller. When you pedal, the pins and rollers rub against each other under heavy load. Grit from the road gets in between them and acts like sandpaper. Over time the pins and rollers wear down, and the gap between them grows.

The chain does not stretch like a rubber band. Its metal parts wear, so each link becomes slightly longer. The chain gets longer in total, and the teeth on the cassette and chainrings no longer match the rollers well.

Lube and cleaning slow this wear. Dry chains and chains full of grit wear faster. Riding in rain, mud, or salty roads speeds things up too.

## How to measure wear

Use a chain checker tool, or a steel ruler.

With a ruler:

1. Pull the chain tight. Hold the ruler along the chain.
2. Measure from the center of one pin to the center of the pin 12 inches away.
3. A new chain measures 12.0 inches. Wear adds length.
4. Take readings at a few spots on the chain, since wear is not always even.

What the numbers mean:

- 0.5 percent wear is about 1/16 inch over 12 inches. Many 10, 11, and 12 speed drivetrains should be serviced by this point to protect the cassette.
- 0.75 percent wear is about 3/32 inch over 12 inches. Many manufacturers call this the replacement point, and older 8 and 9 speed chains can often run this far.

Check your chain manufacturer and cassette manufacturer for exact limits, because they vary.

A chain checker tool gives the same reading with less effort. Some shops use a tool that reads the wear percentage directly.

## When to replace the chain

Replace the chain when it reaches the wear limit above. Replace it sooner if you see any of these signs:

- The chain skips on the cassette, especially under hard pedaling.
- The chain has stiff or rusty links that do not flex.
- A link is damaged, bent, or missing a roller.

Changing the chain early costs less than changing the cassette and chainrings later. Doing it on time is the cheapest way to keep the drivetrain in good shape.

## When to replace the cassette

The cassette is the set of rear cogs. It wears when the chain wears and when the cogs are used past their life.

Signs the cassette needs replacing:

- Teeth look hooked or shark fin shaped, with a pointed back edge on each tooth.
- The chain slips or skips on certain cogs, even after you clean and adjust the derailleur.
- A new chain skips on the worn cassette when you pedal hard.
- Teeth look narrow, thin, or worn down in the middle.

A simple test: put a new chain on the bike and pedal under load in the middle gears. If it skips, the cassette is worn. Replace it.

If you replace the chain before it reaches the limit, the cassette usually lasts much longer. A cassette worn with a stretched chain can ruin a new chain in a short time, so replace both together when the cassette is worn.

## Summary

- Measure the chain every few hundred miles, or after wet rides.
- Replace the chain at about 0.5 to 0.75 percent wear, following the manufacturer.
- Replace the cassette when its teeth hook, or when a new chain skips on it.
- Keep the chain clean and lubed to slow all of this.

# Chain and Cassette Wear

## Why chains wear out

A bicycle chain does not actually stretch. The pins and rollers wear down, and the gap between pins grows. Each link pivots on a pin, and grit that gets past the lubricant grinds the pin and the inner plate. Over time the pitch, which is the distance between pin centers, gets longer. Riding in rain, mud, or sand speeds this up. Too little lubricant or the wrong lubricant does too.

A worn chain also wears the cassette and chainrings faster. The longer chain sits deeper in the teeth and wears their shape into hooks and sharp points.

## How to measure wear

Use a chain checker tool, such as a Park CC-2 or similar. Clip the tool onto the chain, with the hook in a roller, and read the indicator.

Or measure by hand:
1. Use a ruler or steel tape.
2. Measure from the outside edge of one pin to the outside edge of the pin 12 inches away. On a new chain this distance is 12.0 inches.
3. Measure the chain at several spots, since wear is not always even.

A stretch percentage is the measured length minus 12, divided by 12, times 100. For example, a reading of 12.09 inches is 0.75 percent.

## When to replace the chain

- Around 0.5 percent: early wear. Clean and lube the chain well and check it again soon.
- Around 0.75 percent: replace the chain. Most shops use this limit.
- Replace at once if the chain binds, links stiffen, or a link is damaged.

Checking often helps. Replacing a chain at 0.75 percent protects the cassette. Waiting past that point usually means the cassette also needs replacing.

## When to replace the cassette

Replace the cassette when:
- The teeth have hooked or shark-fin shapes, with sharp edges on one side.
- A new chain slips or skips under pedaling load, especially on the largest or smallest cogs.
- Teeth are missing, cracked, or bent.
- The cassette wore with a chain already past 0.75 percent. Install a new chain and new cassette together.

A new chain on an old cassette will skip. A new cassette on a stretched chain wears fast. Replace both together when either is well worn.

## Practical tips

- Clean and lube the chain every 100 to 200 miles in dry conditions, and more often in wet or gritty conditions.
- Wipe off excess lube so it does not collect grit.
- Shift smoothly and avoid heavy pedaling on the largest cog and smallest chainring at the same time, which stresses the chain.

# Chain and Cassette Wear

## Why chains wear out

A bicycle chain is a row of short steel plates joined by pins and rollers. Each time you pedal, the chain bends around the front chainring, the rear cassette, and the derailleur pulleys. Grit from the road gets between the pins and the bushings, and the metal rubs. Over thousands of miles, the pins and bushings wear slightly. Each link gets a little longer, and the chain stretches. The chain does not actually stretch like rubber. The pitch, which is the distance from one pin to the next, grows.

A stretched chain does not sit in the cassette teeth the way it should. The rollers ride up the tooth faces instead of seating in the valleys. That uneven fit then wears the cassette teeth into hooked shapes. A worn chain can wreck a cassette, and a cassette that is worn can also chew up a new chain quickly, so the two parts should be watched together.

What speeds wear: riding in wet or sandy conditions, no lubrication or dirty lubrication, cross chaining (big front with big rear), and high mileage.

## How to measure chain wear

Use a chain checker tool. It is a small gauge with a hook that sits between the rollers.

1. Clean the chain so grit does not affect the reading.
2. Place the chain checker hook into the chain at a roller.
3. If the tool drops in fully and the gauge reads past the wear line, the chain is worn.

Without a chain checker, use a ruler. Measure 12 links, from the center of one pin to the center of the pin 12 pitches away.

- New chain: 152.4 mm (6.00 inches).
- 0.5% stretch: about 153.2 mm.
- 0.75% stretch: about 153.5 mm.
- 1.0% stretch: about 153.9 mm.

Check the manufacturer specification for your chain and drivetrain, because the limit varies by speed. Many 11 and 12 speed chains are rated for replacement at 0.5% to 0.75%.

## When to replace the chain

- Chain checker reads past the wear line, or the 12 link measure reaches about 0.75% stretch.
- Shifting skips or the chain jumps under load, even after adjusting the derailleur.
- Stiff links or visible damage such as cracked plates or bent pins.

Replacing a chain early costs far less than replacing a cassette and chainring. Replacing a chain at about 0.75% usually protects the cassette.

## How to measure cassette wear

The cassette has no simple gauge. Inspect it by eye and by feel.

- Look at the teeth on the largest sprockets. Hooked or shark fin teeth, where the tooth face looks like a hook or sharp ridge, show wear.
- Look at the teeth from the side. Pointed or sharpened teeth are worn.
- Check that a new chain runs without skipping on the cassette under pedaling load.

## When to replace the cassette

- A new chain skips under load on the cassette, even after adjusting the derailleur.
- Teeth are hooked, sharp, or noticeably thinner than the new teeth.
- The cassette was used with a worn chain for a long time.

Always replace the chain first. A new chain on a worn cassette will skip, and a worn chain on a new cassette wears the new cassette fast. Replace the chain and cassette together when both are worn.

## Quick checklist

1. Clean and lubricate the chain regularly.
2. Measure the chain with a checker every few hundred miles.
3. Replace the chain at about 0.75% stretch.
4. Inspect the cassette when replacing the chain.
5. Replace the cassette when a new chain skips.

# Chain and Cassette Wear

## Why chains wear out

A bicycle chain is a row of short steel plates joined by pins and rollers. Each time you pedal, the chain bends around the front chainring, the rear cassette, and the derailleur pulleys. Grit from the road gets between the pins and the bushings, and the metal rubs. Over thousands of miles, the pins and bushings wear slightly. Each link gets a little longer, and the chain stretches. The chain does not actually stretch like rubber. The pitch, which is the distance from one pin to the next, grows.

A stretched chain does not sit in the cassette teeth the way it should. The rollers ride up the tooth faces instead of seating in the valleys. That uneven fit then wears the cassette teeth into hooked shapes. A worn chain can wreck a cassette, and a cassette that is worn can also chew up a new chain quickly, so the two parts should be watched together.

What speeds wear: riding in wet or sandy conditions, no lubrication or dirty lubrication, cross chaining (big front with big rear), and high mileage.

## How to measure chain wear

Use a chain checker tool. It is a small gauge with a hook that sits between the rollers.

1. Clean the chain so grit does not affect the reading.
2. Place the chain checker hook into the chain at a roller.
3. If the tool drops in fully and the gauge reads past the wear line, the chain is worn.

Without a chain checker, use a ruler. Measure 12 links, from the center of one pin to the center of the pin 12 pitches away.

- New chain: 152.4 mm (6.00 inches).
- 0.5% stretch: about 153.2 mm.
- 0.75% stretch: about 153.5 mm.
- 1.0% stretch: about 153.9 mm.

Check the manufacturer specification for your chain and drivetrain, because the limit varies by speed. Many 11 and 12 speed chains are rated for replacement at 0.5% to 0.75%.

## When to replace the chain

- Chain checker reads past the wear line, or the 12 link measure reaches about 0.75% stretch.
- Shifting skips or the chain jumps under load, even after adjusting the derailleur.
- Stiff links or visible damage such as cracked plates or bent pins.

Replacing a chain early costs far less than replacing a cassette and chainring. Replacing a chain at about 0.75% usually protects the cassette.

## How to measure cassette wear

The cassette has no simple gauge. Inspect it by eye and by feel.

- Look at the teeth on the largest sprockets. Hooked or shark fin teeth, where the tooth face looks like a hook or sharp ridge, show wear.
- Look at the teeth from the side. Pointed or sharpened teeth are worn.
- Check that a new chain runs without skipping on the cassette under pedaling load.

## When to replace the cassette

- A new chain skips under load on the cassette, even after adjusting the derailleur.
- Teeth are hooked, sharp, or noticeably thinner than the new teeth.
- The cassette was used with a worn chain for a long time.

Always replace the chain first. A new chain on a worn cassette will skip, and a worn chain on a new cassette wears the new cassette fast. Replace the chain and cassette together when both are worn.

## Quick checklist

1. Clean and lubricate the chain regularly.
2. Measure the chain with a checker every few hundred miles.
3. Replace the chain at about 0.75% stretch.
4. Inspect the cassette when replacing the chain.
5. Replace the cassette when a new chain skips.

# Brake Check Procedure for New Volunteers

Fern Hollow Bicycle Cooperative

Use this checklist before any bike with brakes leaves the shop. Do the rim brake section for bikes with rim brakes and the disc brake section for bikes with disc brakes. Check the front and rear brake on every bike.

If anything fails a check, do not release the bike. Tag it "DO NOT RIDE" and tell a shop lead.

## Before you start

1. Stand the bike in the stand or flip it upright on a clean floor.
2. Spin each wheel by hand. Note any side-to-side wobble or rubbing.
3. Check that quick releases or thru axles are fully closed and the wheel is seated square in the dropouts.

## Part A: Rim brakes

A1. Pad condition
- Look at each brake pad. Replace it if the wear groove is gone or the rubber is cracked, hard, or glazed.
- Check that the pad is not split from its holder.

A2. Pad alignment
- The pad must hit the rim, not the tire or the rim edge.
- Set the front edge of each pad 1 to 2 mm closer to the rim than the back edge. This is called toe-in. It makes the brake squeal less and stop more evenly.
- Tighten the pad bolt and recheck alignment after tightening.

A3. Bolts and cables
- Check that the brake arm pivot bolt, the cable pinch bolt, and the pad bolts are tight.
- Check the cable for fraying, kinks, or rust. Replace a frayed cable.
- Check that the cable housing ends are not cracked and the housing is not too short or long at the handlebars or frame.

A4. Centering

# Week-Long Bike Tour Packing Guide

This guide lists what to pack for a seven-day bike tour, with the reason for each item. Pack in the order shown so the heavy and bulky gear sits low and close to the bike.

## 1. Bike and Repair Kit

Bring these in your bags or on the bike. Most tour breakdowns are flats or small mechanical faults, so this section matters most.

1. Spare inner tubes, two at minimum. Reason: a single flat with no spare can end your day. Carry tubes sized to your wheels.
2. Tire levers, three. Reason: they remove a tire bead on the roadside. Plastic levers avoid scratching rims.
3. Mini pump or CO2 inflator with spare cartridges. Reason: you need to reinflate after a patch. Test the pump before you leave.
4. Multi-tool with hex keys, screwdriver, and chain tool. Reason: it covers seat, handlebar, and brake adjustments.
5. Patch kit and tire boot. Reason: a tear in the tire wall can be fixed with a boot, which saves a spare tube.
6. Chain links or a quick-link. Reason: a broken chain needs a replacement link to get moving again.
7. Small bottle of chain lube and a rag. Reason: a dry chain squeaks, wears fast, and shifts poorly.
8. Spare brake pads, if your bike uses rim brakes or you have a known wear issue. Reason: worn pads reduce stopping power on long descents.
9. Spoke wrench and a few spare spokes if your bike is older. Reason: a loose or broken spoke can make a wheel unsafe.

## 2. Safety and Visibility

1. Helmet. Reason: required on most tours and the most important protection you carry.
2. Front white light and rear red light, both charged. Reason: lights keep you visible to drivers in early morning, dusk, and tunnels.
3. Reflective vest or bands. Reason: they add visibility on busy roads.
4. Cycling gloves. Reason: they protect your hands in a fall and reduce numbness on long rides.
5. Sunglasses, ideally with clear or amber lenses for low light. Reason: they block UV and keep bugs and grit out of your eyes.

## 3. Clothing

Pack for layers. Weather on tour often changes within one day.

1. Two to three pairs of padded cycling shorts. Reason: you ride most days, and padding reduces saddle soreness. Rotating pairs lets each one dry.
2. Three to four cycling jerseys or quick-dry tops. Reason: they wick sweat and dry overnight.
3. One long-sleeve base layer. Reason: it warms you on cold mornings and descents.
4. Lightweight rain jacket and rain pants or leg covers. Reason: a wet day without rain gear makes you cold and slow.
5. Warm layer, such as a fleece or insulated jacket. Reason: temperatures drop sharply after dark and at high elevation.
6. Arm warmers or leg warmers. Reason: they add warmth without much bulk and can be removed as you warm up.
7. Socks, five to seven pairs of cycling socks. Reason: clean, dry socks prevent blisters and odor.
8. Off-bike clothes: one pair of pants or shorts, two casual shirts, and one pair of comfortable shoes. Reason: you need dry clothes for evenings and rest stops.
9. Underwear, one pair per day plus one spare. Reason: clean underwear prevents chafing.
10. Sleepwear. Reason: you need warm, dry clothes for the night.
11. Hat or cap for under the helmet, and a buff or neck gaiter. Reason: they keep sweat out of your eyes and protect your neck from sun.

## 4. Shoes

1. Cycling shoes or your usual riding shoes. Reason: they must fit well for seven days of pedaling.
2. Sandals or light shoes for camp or rest days. Reason: they let your feet breathe after riding.

## 5. Camping and Sleep Gear (if you camp)

1. Tent, sleeping bag rated for the coldest night expected, and sleeping pad. Reason: a pad insulates you from the ground and a bag rated for cold keeps you warm.
2. Pillow or inflatable pillow. Reason: a better pillow improves rest after long days.
3. Headlamp with spare batteries. Reason: you need hands-free light for camp chores after dark.

## 6. Toiletries and Health

1. Sunscreen, SPF 30 or higher, and lip balm with SPF. Reason: long hours in sun cause burns even on cloudy days.
2. Chamois cream. Reason: it reduces friction and chafing in the saddle area.
3. Personal medications in original containers. Reason: keeping them labeled avoids problems at border or security checks.
4. Basic first aid kit with bandages, antiseptic wipes, blister treatment, pain relief, and electrolyte tablets. Reason: you will treat scrapes and blisters on the road.
5. Hand sanitizer, toothbrush, toothpaste, and a small towel. Reason: hygiene matters when water and showers are limited.
6. Insect repellent. Reason: it protects against bites on rural routes.
7. Travel-size soap and shampoo. Reason: they are light and do the job.

## 7. Food, Water, and Navigation

1. Water bottles or hydration bladder, at least two liters capacity. Reason: you need water between towns in hot weather.
2. Water filter or purification tablets if your route has unreliable water. Reason: they make stream or tap water safe.
3. Snacks such as bars, nuts, or dried fruit. Reason: you burn many calories and need quick energy between meals.
4. Phone with offline maps saved for the whole route. Reason: coverage drops in rural areas.
5. Phone mount for the handlebar. Reason: it keeps navigation visible while riding.
6. Power bank and charging cables. Reason: your phone runs down fast from GPS and camera use.
7. Paper map or route sheet. Reason: it works when batteries die.

## 8. Documents and Money

1. Passport or ID, plus copies stored separately. Reason: lost documents are hard to replace on the road.
2. Cash in local currency, and one or two payment cards. Reason: some small towns and rural shops accept cash only.
3. Travel insurance details and emergency contacts. Reason: they speed up help after an accident.
4. Copy of your bike shop or repair contact list for the route. Reason: local shops may be far apart.

## 9. Bags and Organization

1. Panniers or a rear rack bag, with waterproof liners. Reason: waterproof liners keep clothes dry in rain and when a bag falls in a puddle.
2. Handlebar bag for snacks, phone, and documents you need quickly. Reason: you reach them without stopping.
3. Stuff sacks or packing cubes. Reason: they separate clean and dirty clothes and compress bulk.
4. Reflective or brightly colored bag covers. Reason: they add visibility on the bike.

## 10. Packing Tips

1. Balance the load. Put heavy items low and evenly between left and right panniers. Reason: uneven loads make the bike unstable.
2. Keep tools and repair items in the handlebar bag or top of a pannier. Reason: you need them fast when a problem stops you.
3. Test everything before you leave. Ride with the full load for one or two days. Reason: this reveals fit and handling issues early.
4. Weigh your luggage, and remove anything you did not use on the test ride. Reason: extra weight tires you on climbs.

## 11. Before You Fly

1. Remove or pack CO2 cartridges, lithium batteries, and tools in accordance with your airline rules. Reason: airlines restrict these items in checked and carry-on bags.
2. Pack the bike in a box or hard case with padding. Reason: protects frame and components in transit.
3. Remove pedals, turn the handlebars, and deflate tires slightly if your airline requires it. Reason: this reduces damage to the bike and helps it fit cases.
4. Check your airline's bike policy, including fees and size limits, before you book. Reason: rules and fees vary widely.

11. Hat or cap for under the helmet, and a buff or neck gaiter. Reason: they keep sweat out of your eyes and protect your neck from sun.

## 4. Shoes

1. Cycling shoes or your usual riding shoes. Reason: they must fit well for seven days of pedaling.
2. Sandals or light shoes for camp or rest days. Reason: they let your feet breathe after riding.

## 5. Camping and Sleep Gear (if you camp)

1. Tent, sleeping bag rated for the coldest night expected, and sleeping pad. Reason: a pad insulates you from the ground and a bag rated for cold keeps you warm.
2. Pillow or inflatable pillow. Reason: a better pillow improves rest after long days.
3. Headlamp with spare batteries. Reason: you need hands-free light for camp chores after dark.

## 6. Toiletries and Health

1. Sunscreen, SPF 30 or higher, and lip balm with SPF. Reason: long hours in sun cause burns even on cloudy days.
2. Chamois cream. Reason: it reduces friction and chafing in the saddle area.
3. Personal medications in original containers. Reason: keeping them labeled avoids problems at border or security checks.
4. Basic first aid kit with bandages, antiseptic wipes, blister treatment, pain relief, and electrolyte tablets. Reason: you will treat scrapes and blisters on the road.
5. Hand sanitizer, toothbrush, toothpaste, and a small towel. Reason: hygiene matters when water and showers are limited.
6. Insect repellent. Reason: it protects against bites on rural routes.
7. Travel-size soap and shampoo. Reason: they are light and do the job.

## 7. Food, Water, and Navigation

1. Water bottles or hydration bladder, at least two liters capacity. Reason: you need water between towns in hot weather.
2. Water filter or purification tablets if your route has unreliable water. Reason: they make stream or tap water safe.
3. Snacks such as bars, nuts, or dried fruit. Reason: you burn many calories and need quick energy between meals.
4. Phone with offline maps saved for the whole route. Reason: coverage drops in rural areas.
5. Phone mount for the handlebar. Reason: it keeps navigation visible while riding.
6. Power bank and charging cables. Reason: your phone runs down fast from GPS and camera use.
7. Paper map or route sheet. Reason: it works when batteries die.

## 8. Documents and Money

1. Passport or ID, plus copies stored separately. Reason: lost documents are hard to replace on the road.
2. Cash in local currency, and one or two payment cards. Reason: some small towns and rural shops accept cash only.
3. Travel insurance details and emergency contacts. Reason: they speed up help after an accident.
4. Copy of your bike shop or repair contact list for the route. Reason: local shops may be far apart.

## 9. Bags and Organization

1. Panniers or a rear rack bag, with waterproof liners. Reason: waterproof liners keep clothes dry in rain and when a bag falls in a puddle.
2. Handlebar bag for snacks, phone, and documents you need quickly. Reason: you reach them without stopping.
3. Stuff sacks or packing cubes. Reason: they separate clean and dirty clothes and compress bulk.
4. Reflective or brightly colored bag covers. Reason: they add visibility on the bike.

## 10. Packing Tips

1. Balance the load. Put heavy items low and evenly between left and right panniers. Reason: uneven loads make the bike unstable.
2. Keep tools and repair items in the handlebar bag or top of a pannier. Reason: you need them fast when a problem stops you.
3. Test everything before you leave. Ride with the full load for one or two days. Reason: this reveals fit and handling issues early.
4. Weigh your luggage, and remove anything you did not use on the test ride. Reason: extra weight tires you on climbs.

## 11. Before You Fly

1. Remove or pack CO2 cartridges, lithium batteries, and tools in accordance with your airline rules. Reason: airlines restrict these items in checked and carry-on bags.
2. Pack the bike in a box or hard case with padding. Reason: protects frame and components in transit.
3. Remove pedals, turn the handlebars, and deflate tires slightly if your airline requires it. Reason: this reduces damage to the bike and helps it fit cases.
4. Check your airline's bike policy, including fees and size limits, before you book. Reason: rules and fees vary widely.

# Chain and Cassette Wear

## Why chains wear out

A bike chain is a row of small steel plates and rollers. Each link pivots on pins, and every pedal stroke bends and straightens those joints under load. Grit from the road gets into the pin joints. Abrasive grit grinds the pins and bushings, so each link slowly gets longer. The chain does not stretch like rubber. The pins wear, and the gap between pins grows. This is called chain elongation.

Wear speeds up with:
- Riding in rain, mud, or sand without cleaning
- Little or no lubrication, or lube that picked up grit and turned to paste
- High power and hard shifting under load
- Narrow or worn chainrings and cogs, which make the chain ride unevenly

## How to measure wear

Use a chain checker, a tool with a hooked pin that drops into a link. Use a ruler if you have no checker.

1. Clean the chain and the drivetrain so the measurement is not thrown off by grime.
2. Pull the chain away from the chainring and lay a ruler along the chain.
3. Measure across exactly 12 inches (or 24 links, 12 full pitches). A new chain measures 12.000 inches between the outer edges of pin 1 and pin 13.
4. Check several spots around the chain. Wear is not always even.

Reading the result:
- 12.00 to 12.05 inches (0.5 percent): new or nearly new
- About 12.25 inches (0.75 percent): worn. Plan to replace it soon, because the cassette wears faster if you keep riding it.
- 12.50 inches (1 percent): worn out. Replace the chain now.

Some chain checkers use a 0.5 and 0.75 scale instead. A checker that reads 0.75 means replace the chain.

## When to replace the chain

Replace the chain at 0.75 percent wear, or sooner if you see any of these:
- Skipping or slipping under power, especially on the largest or smallest cog
- Visible rust, stiff links that do not flex, or rollers that do not turn freely
- Bent or damaged plates
- Shifting that feels rough even after adjustment

If you wait past 1 percent, the cassette and chainrings will likely wear too, and replacing only the chain may not fix the skipping.

Always replace the chain with the same speed chain you have, for example 9, 10, 11, or 12 speed. A chain that does not match the cassette width will shift poorly.

## When to replace the cassette

The cassette is the set of cogs on the rear wheel. Its teeth wear to a hooked shape as the chain wears in. A worn cassette tends to make a new chain skip.

Replace the cassette when:
- The chain is past 0.75 percent wear and you have a worn chain that skips even after a new chain is fitted
- Teeth look hooked, shark-fin shaped, or have sharp points
- Teeth are pointed or narrowed on one side
- The chain skips on the largest or most used cogs

Good practice: replace the chain before it reaches 0.75 percent, so the cassette lasts longer. Replacing a chain every time it hits 0.5 to 0.75 percent is much cheaper than replacing a cassette.

When you replace the cassette, check the chainrings too. If the chain is worn, the chainring teeth may also be worn, and a new chain on old rings will skip.

## Short version for the class

- Chains stretch because the pins and bushings wear from grit and load.
- Measure across 12 inches. Replace the chain at about 0.75 percent, which reads about 12.25 inches.
- Replace the cassette when its teeth look hooked, or when a new chain still skips.
- Clean and lube often to slow all of this down.
