files.workbench/chain_wear_guide.md:
# Bicycle Chain and Cassette Wear

## Why chains wear out

A bicycle chain is a row of outer plates, inner plates, pins, and rollers. Each pin sits inside a bushing, and each roller turns around the outside of a bushing. Every time you pedal, these parts rub under high force. Tiny amounts of metal wear away at the contact points, so the gap between pins grows slightly. Engineers call this pitch elongation. The chain does not really stretch like rubber. It gets longer because the joints wear.

Several things speed up wear:
- Grit and sand that get into the chain and act like sandpaper.
- Dry or unlubricated chains.
- Wet riding, which washes lubricant away.
- Cross-chaining, which is running the chain at a steep angle between the largest front gear and the largest rear gear. It puts extra side load on the chain.
- Heavy loads, hard climbs, and high power output.
- Cheap chains with soft metal or poor tolerances.

## How to measure chain wear

Use a chain wear indicator tool. These are inexpensive and give a reliable reading.

1. Clean the chain so grit does not affect the reading.
2. Place the tool's hooks into the rollers of the chain, and check the reading on the scale.
3. Check at several points around the chain, since wear is not always even.

If you have no tool, use a ruler:
1. Measure 12 full links, from the center of one pin to the center of the 12th pin after it. A new chain reads exactly 12.00 inches, or 304.8 mm.
2. Compare the reading with the table below.
3. Measure in more than one spot and use the worst reading.

| Wear | 12-link length (inches) | 12-link length (mm) | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.0% | 12.00 | 304.8 | New |
| 0.5% | 12.06 | 306.3 | Early wear. Watch it closely. |
| 0.75% | 12.09 | 307.1 | Replace the chain now. |
| 1.0% | 12.12 | 307.8 | Worn. Replacing it late can damage the cassette and chainrings. |

A ruler reads rough numbers. A wear tool is more accurate, and it is the better choice if you measure often.

## When to replace the chain

- Replace the chain at about 0.75% wear. Waiting longer usually costs more because the worn chain damages the cassette and chainrings.
- Replace it sooner if the chain is stiff, rusty, or has stiff links.
- Replace it sooner if you ride in harsh conditions and the chain looks dry, dirty, or gritty.
- Replace it at 0.5% if you want the drivetrain to last longest. This is common practice for mountain bikes and for riders who use 11-speed or narrower chains.

## When to replace the cassette

The cassette is the set of rear sprockets. Its teeth wear to match the chain, so the two parts are best replaced together.

Replace the cassette when:
- The teeth look hooked or shark-fin shaped, with one side of each tooth sharply pointed.
- A new chain skips or jumps under pedaling load, even after you adjust the derailleur.
- The chain has worn past about 1% and you have already fitted a new chain, which now skips on the worn teeth.
- Teeth are chipped, bent, or missing.

If you replace a chain at 0.75% or earlier, the cassette usually lasts through several chains.

## Quick tips to slow wear

- Clean and lubricate the chain after wet rides, and about every 100 to 200 miles in dry conditions.
- Wipe off excess lubricant. A dry-looking chain is ready to ride, and extra oil only attracts grit.
- Avoid cross-chaining.
- Check wear once a month if you ride often.
- Keep a record of when you installed each chain, so you know how long it lasted.

## Summary for reading aloud

Chains wear because the pins and rollers rub and the joints get looser over time. Measure wear with a chain checker, or by measuring 12 links with a ruler, where a new chain reads 12 inches. Replace the chain at about three-quarters of a percent wear. Replace the cassette when its teeth look hooked or when a new chain skips under load.

# Bicycle Chain and Cassette Wear

## Why chains wear out

A bicycle chain is a row of outer plates, inner plates, pins, and rollers. Each pin sits inside a bushing, and each roller turns around the outside of a bushing. Every time you pedal, these parts rub under high force. Tiny amounts of metal wear away at the contact points, so the gap between pins grows slightly. Engineers call this pitch elongation. The chain does not really stretch like rubber. It gets longer because the joints wear.

Several things speed up wear:
- Grit and sand that get into the chain and act like sandpaper.
- Dry or unlubricated chains.
- Wet riding, which washes lubricant away.
- Cross-chaining, which is running the chain at a steep angle between the largest front gear and the largest rear gear. It puts extra side load on the chain.
- Heavy loads, hard climbs, and high power output.
- Cheap chains with soft metal or poor tolerances.

## How to measure chain wear

Use a chain wear indicator tool. These are inexpensive and give a reliable reading.

1. Clean the chain so grit does not affect the reading.
2. Place the tool's hooks into the rollers of the chain, and check the reading on the scale.
3. Check at several points around the chain, since wear is not always even.

If you have no tool, use a ruler:
1. Measure 12 full links, from the center of one pin to the center of the 12th pin after it. A new chain reads exactly 12.00 inches, or 304.8 mm.
2. Compare the reading with the table below.
3. Measure in more than one spot and use the worst reading.

| Wear | 12-link length (inches) | 12-link length (mm) | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.0% | 12.00 | 304.8 | New |
| 0.5% | 12.06 | 306.3 | Early wear. Watch it closely. |
| 0.75% | 12.09 | 307.1 | Replace the chain now. |
| 1.0% | 12.12 | 307.8 | Worn. Replacing it late can damage the cassette and chainrings. |

## When to replace the chain

- Replace it sooner if the chain is stiff, rusty, or has stiff links.
- Replace it sooner if you ride in harsh conditions and the chain looks dry, dirty, or gritty.
- Replace it at 0.5% if you want the drivetrain to last longest. This is common practice for mountain bikes and for riders who use 11-speed or narrower chains.

## When to replace the cassette

The cassette is the set of rear sprockets. Its teeth wear to match the chain, so the two parts are best replaced together.

Replace the cassette when:
- The teeth look hooked or shark-fin shaped, with one side of each tooth sharply pointed.
- A new chain skips or jumps under pedaling load, even after you adjust the derailleur.
- The chain has worn past about 1% and you have already fitted a new chain, which now skips on the worn teeth.
- Teeth are chipped, bent, or missing.

If you replace a chain at 0.75% or earlier, the cassette usually lasts through several chains.

# Week-Long Bike Tour Packing Guide

This guide lists what to pack for a seven-day self-supported bike tour, with the reason for each item. Adjust quantities for weather, route length, and how much you carry in a pannier.

## 1. Bike and repair kit (carry on the bike)

- Spare tubes, two or three, sized to your tire (for example 700c). Reason: a flat on the road is the most common delay, and a patch kit alone is slower and fails more often.
- Tire levers, two or three. Reason: needed to remove a tire from the rim for a tube swap.
- Compact pump or CO2 inflator with spare cartridges. Reason: you need a way to reinflate after a flat.
- Multi-tool with chain breaker, hex keys, and screwdriver. Reason: covers most adjustments and chain repairs.
- Chain quick link (matched to your chain speed) and a chain tool. Reason: a broken chain stops the tour without a fix.
- Spoke wrench sized to your wheels. Reason: a loose or broken spoke can make a wheel unrideable.
- Patch kit. Reason: backup for tire punctures that a tube swap cannot solve.
- Derailleur hanger spare, if your frame uses a replaceable hanger. Reason: a bent hanger misaligns the gears and is hard to find on tour.
- Brake pad spares and a small amount of cable. Reason: worn pads or a snapped cable can make braking unsafe.
- Lube for chain and a rag. Reason: a dry chain wears fast and gets noisy, and a rag keeps grease off your clothes.

## 2. Safety and visibility

- Helmet. Reason: required for head protection in a fall or collision.
- Front white light and rear red light, both charged, plus spare batteries. Reason: legal and practical visibility on early or late riding.
- Reflective vest or ankle bands. Reason: drivers see moving reflective material from further away.
- Mirror on the helmet or handlebar. Reason: lets you check traffic without turning your head.

## 3. Clothing

- Cycling shorts, two or three pairs with padded liners. Reason: padding reduces saddle pressure over long days, and a second pair lets one dry while you ride the other.
- Cycling jerseys, three or four. Reason: moisture-wicking fabric dries on the body overnight.
- Lightweight long-sleeve layer. Reason: cold mornings and descents.
- Rain jacket and rain pants or leg covers. Reason: wet weather is the main cause of cold-related stress on tour.
- Warm layer, such as a fleece or light down jacket. Reason: evenings and high passes are much colder than the daytime high.
- Cycling gloves, one pair plus a backup pair. Reason: padded gloves protect your hands from numbness, and a spare keeps you warm if the first pair gets soaked.
- Warm hat or buff, and a sun hat or cap. Reason: each covers a different weather condition.
- Two pairs of socks suited to cycling, plus a warm pair for camp. Reason: dry feet prevent blisters and cold toes.
- Sandals or light camp shoes. Reason: lets your feet breathe and gives you something to wear off the bike.
- Sunglasses, with a spare lens if you ride in bright conditions. Reason: protect your eyes from wind, insects, and glare.

## 4. Sleep and camp

- Tent or bivy, with stakes and a footprint. Reason: shelter that matches the campsites on your route.
- Sleeping bag rated for the coldest night you expect. Reason: a bag that is too warm is easy to vent, but one that is too cold is not.
- Sleeping pad. Reason: insulates you from the ground and cushions your body after long days.
- Pillow, inflatable or stuff sack with clothes. Reason: improves sleep quality after hard riding.
- Headlamp with spare batteries. Reason: hands-free light for camp chores and night toilet trips.

## 5. Cooking and water

- Stove, fuel, and a lighter or matches. Reason: hot food and drinks are needed on days when shops are closed or far apart.
- Pot, bowl, utensils, and a small cutting knife. Reason: these are the minimum tools for preparing meals.
- Two water bottles or a hydration bladder, plus a filter or purification tablets. Reason: you need about 0.5 to 1 liter per hour of riding in warm weather, and water sources along the route are not always safe.
- Food stored in sealed bags. Reason: keeps food dry and keeps scent away from animals at camp.

## 6. Documents, money, and phone

- ID, insurance card, and emergency contact list in a waterproof bag. Reason: needed for hospital care and for border or hotel check-in.
- Cash in small bills and a card. Reason: some rural shops and campsites accept cash only.
- Phone with a charger, a power bank, and cables. Reason: navigation, maps, and emergency calls depend on battery life.
- Offline maps and the route file downloaded before the trip. Reason: cell service is unreliable in rural areas.
- Printed or written copy of the route and key phone numbers. Reason: a backup if the phone fails or dies.

## 7. Personal items

- Sunscreen, lip balm, and insect repellent. Reason: sun and insects are constant on long days outdoors.
- Toiletries in small travel sizes. Reason: keeps weight low while covering daily hygiene.
- Personal first-aid kit: bandages, antiseptic wipes, blister pads, pain relief, and any prescription medicine. Reason: blisters, road rash, and aches are common on tour.
- Quick-dry towel. Reason: dries faster than a cotton towel and packs small.
- Earplugs and an eye mask. Reason: help you sleep in noisy campsites or early-rising towns.

## 8. Packing and bag setup

- Two or three panniers or a bikepacking setup. Reason: spreads weight low and balanced for stable steering.
- Dry bags or pannier liners. Reason: keep your gear dry if rain hits or if you cross water.

# Week-Long Bike Tour Packing Guide

Assumptions: a 7-night tour with bags carried on the bike, mixed weather, one flight with a bike box, and laundry available every 2 to 3 days. Adjust quantities if your tour is supported or your climate is different.

## 1. Bike and flight prep
- Bike box or hard case: protects the frame and derailleur from baggage handling. Reason: an unprotected derailleur hanger bends easily and can end the trip.
- Pedals removed, handlebars turned or removed, seat post dropped and wrapped: these save space and reduce the chance of damage.
- Derailleur hanger spare: a spare hanger matched to your frame. Reason: it is the single most common part to fail in transit.
- Tire levers, spare tubes (2), patch kit, mini pump or CO2 with heads: enough to fix two flats without a shop.
- Multi-tool with chain breaker, quick link, spare brake pads: covers chain repairs and worn pads on a long descent.
- Spoke wrench and a few spare spokes if your wheels are built for touring. Reason: broken spokes on a loaded bike are common.
- Chain lube (small bottle, carried in checked luggage only if the airline allows liquids).
- Check the airline bike policy and the bike box fee before you leave.

## 2. Clothing (worn or packed)
- Cycling shorts: 2 pairs. Reason: one pair can be washed and dried while you wear the other.
- Cycling jerseys: 3. Reason: one per two riding days keeps you comfortable without overpacking.
- Base layer (merino or synthetic): 1. Reason: it dries fast and handles cold mornings and descents.
- Warm layer (light fleece or insulated jacket): 1. Reason: mountain passes and early mornings are often 10 degrees colder than the valley.
- Rain jacket, packable: 1. Reason: rain on a long day is harder to escape than on a short ride.
- Arm warmers and leg warmers: 1 pair each, optional. Reason: they cover temperature swings without adding much bulk.
- Casual clothes: 1 set of shirt and trousers or shorts for evenings and off-bike time.
- Socks: 4 cycling pairs and 1 warm pair for evenings. Reason: wet feet cause blisters.
- Underwear: 5 pairs. Reason: enough for 7 days with one laundry stop.
- Sleepwear: 1 set. Reason: needed for hotel or hostel nights.
- Hat or cap, sun gloves, and a buff or neck gaiter. Reason: sun and wind exposure add up over long days.
- Cycling shoes or your riding shoes, plus one lightweight pair of walking shoes or sandals. Reason: you need dry shoes for the evening.

## 3. Health and comfort
- Chamois cream: prevents chafing on long days.
- Sunscreen SPF 50, lip balm with SPF: sun exposure on the bike is intense.
- Basic first aid: plasters, antiseptic wipes, blister pads, pain relief, and any personal prescriptions in original packaging. Reason: road rash and blisters are the most common injuries on tour.
- Electrolyte tablets: prevents cramps and fatigue in heat.
- Travel documents, insurance details, and a copy of your passport. Reason: a lost passport on tour can stop the trip.
- Headlamp and front and rear lights, with spare batteries or a charger. Reason: a late arrival in the dark needs lights, and most flights and hotels do not include them.
- Reflective vest or ankle bands: keeps you visible on quiet roads.
- Earplugs and eye mask: help with sleep in shared or noisy rooms.

## 4. Electronics
- Phone, charger, and a short cable: navigation and emergency calls.
- Power bank (10,000 mAh or more): charges phone and lights between stops.
- Bike computer or GPS and its mount, if you use one. Reason: a mount that fails on a rough road can drop the device.
- Offline maps downloaded before you fly. Reason: you will not reliably get data on the road.
- Adapter for the destination country.

## 5. Bags and organization
- Two panniers or a rear rack bag and a front bag, with a dry bag liner. Reason: waterproof liners keep clothes dry in rain and river crossings.
- Handlebar bag for snacks, phone, wallet, and documents you need quickly.
- Stuff sacks or packing cubes, one per clothing type. Reason: they speed up packing each morning.
- Padlock or cable lock for stops and hotel storage.
- Small toiletries kit in a leakproof bag. Reason: a leak from a bottle can soak the whole bag.

## 6. Food and water
- Water bottles: 2 cages and 2 bottles. Reason: heat and climbs can exhaust 1 litre quickly.
- Water filter or purification tablets if your route passes rural areas.
- Snacks: energy bars or similar. Reason: gaps between shops can be long.
- Money: local currency in small notes plus a card. Reason: some rural towns do not accept cards.

## 7. Laundry and daily routine
- Small bottle of travel detergent or sink soap. Reason: quick washing of cycling kit each evening.
- Clothesline or a few elastic cords. Reason: hotels rarely have drying space for wet kit.
- Daily check: tire pressure, chain, brakes, and bolts each morning. Reason: a 2-minute check prevents most roadside failures.

## 8. Packing order
1. Put tools and spare tubes in the bike bag first, where you can reach them.
2. Pack heavy items low and near the centre of the bags to keep the bike stable.
3. Keep rain gear, the warm layer, and phone chargers in the top or handlebar bag for quick access.
4. Weigh each bag before departure. Reason: airline limits and a balanced bike both matter.

## 9. Before you leave
- Test-fit the bike in the box, or assemble it at home once to confirm it goes back together.
- Fly with a printed copy of the bike policy and the route for the first two days.
- Save the bike shop contact for the first stop and the nearest emergency number.

A basic brake check has three parts:

1. **Pads and braking surfaces:** Inspect the brake pads for wear and check that the rotor or rim is clean and true.
2. **Cable or hydraulic system:** Check cable tension and housing, or look for leaks and a firm lever feel on hydraulic brakes.
3. **Function test:** Squeeze each lever and roll the bike. Both brakes should engage smoothly, stop the wheel, and release fully without rubbing.

Typical values (Nm):
- Stem and handlebar clamp: 5 to 6, prevents slip and carbon crush
- Seatpost and saddle clamp: 5 to 6, holds the post without crushing the frame
- Disc caliper mounts: 6 to 8, keeps the caliper aligned
- Rotor bolts: 4 to 6, prevents rotor wobble
- Crank bolt: 35 to 50, seats the crank on the spindle
- Bottom bracket: 35 to 50 for threaded shells
- Pedals: 35 to 40, prevents loosening while pedaling
- Cassette lockring: 30 to 50
- Through axle: 15 to 20, check the hub spec

# Torque wrench reference for a bicycle

## What a torque wrench is for

A torque wrench measures how hard you turn a fastener. A bolt clamps parts together by stretching slightly, and the clamp force depends on the torque you apply and the friction in the threads. Torque is the proxy you can measure.

Too little torque lets parts slip, rattle, or come loose on the ride. Too much torque can crush carbon fiber, stretch or strip aluminum threads, deform a seatpost or stem, or snap a bolt. Carbon parts fail this way most often, and their failures often show no warning before they break.

A click type wrench releases at a preset value, so you stop turning when you hear the click. A beam type wrench shows the value on a scale as you pull. A digital wrench shows the live reading and often beeps at the target.

How to use one:

* Fit the bit or socket fully before you pull, so the bit does not slip off the fastener.
* Pull smoothly on the grip, not on the end of the handle.
* Stop at the click. Do not keep turning after it releases.
* Set the wrench back to a lower value when you store it, so the spring does not stay loaded.

Units: bike specs use newton meters (Nm). Small bolts are sometimes listed in inch pounds (in lbf). One Nm equals about 8.85 in lbf.

Thread condition matters. Dry threads and greased threads produce different clamp force for the same torque. Many specs assume the threads are clean and dry unless the spec says to grease or use thread lock. Carbon parts often say to use a specific lubricant or none at all. Follow the part's own spec.

The values below are typical ranges. The number printed on the component or in the manufacturer's manual overrides them. Where a part has a printed maximum, never go above it.

## Common values across a bike, and why

### Cockpit

* Stem faceplate bolts: 5 to 6 Nm. These clamp the steerer tube. Too much torque cracks carbon steerers and can crush aluminum ones. Too little lets the stem rotate or slip under braking.
* Handlebar clamp bolts: 5 to 6 Nm. Many carbon bars print a 5 or 6 Nm maximum. Over that value, the bar can crack at the clamp. Under it, the bar can twist.
* Brake and shifter lever clamp bolts: 2 to 5 Nm. The lever can slip on the bar if loose. Too much crushes the bar or the lever body.
* Stem top cap or expander bolt: follow the stem spec. These set headset preload and lock the steerer plug. Overtightening the top cap can damage the headset bearings.

### Saddle and seatpost

* Seatpost clamp: 5 to 6 Nm. Holds the post at the height you set. Carbon posts crack if overtightened. A loose clamp lets the post sink or rotate.
* Saddle rail clamp: 5 to 7 Nm. Holds the saddle angle. Loose rails let the saddle tilt, and tight rails can crack carbon rails.

### Brakes

* Caliper mount bolts: 6 to 8 Nm. These keep the caliper square to the rotor. A loose caliper rubs, chatters, and can move under hard braking.
* Disc rotor bolts (6 bolt pattern): 2.5 to 4 Nm. The rotor is thin, so low torque prevents warping. Loose bolts let the rotor wobble, which makes the brakes pulse.
* Center lock rotor lockring: usually about 40 Nm, using a dedicated lockring tool. Holds the rotor against the hub.
* Rim brake caliper bolts: follow the caliper spec, usually 5 to 6 Nm. Loose bolts let the caliper shift toward the rim.

### Wheels

* Thru axle: 8 to 15 Nm, varies by brand. Holds the wheel in the dropouts. A loose axle lets the wheel move and can damage the dropouts.
* Quick release: not a torque setting. Set the cam lever closing force by feel, and leave a clear mark on the lever for the correct closing position.

### Drivetrain

* Crank arm bolt (Shimano Hollowtech, SRAM, and similar): 35 to 55 Nm, varies by brand. Holds the crank on the spindle. Undertightening causes creaking and can damage the crank interface. Overtightening can deform the crank.
* Pedals: 30 to 35 Nm. Right pedal threads tighten clockwise. Left pedal threads are reverse, so they tighten counterclockwise. The pedaling motion keeps the pedals tight, so a loose pedal wears the threads quickly.
* Bottom bracket cups (threaded): 35 to 50 Nm, varies by brand and frame material. Loose cups creak. Overtightening can damage the threads in the frame.
* Press fit bottom brackets: follow the frame spec. Press fit shells have their own fitting method.
* Cassette lockring: 30 to 50 Nm. Holds the cogs against the freehub body. A loose cassette skips under load and wears the teeth.
* Chainring bolts: 8 to 12 Nm. Loose bolts let the chainring shift. Overtightened bolts can strip the crank threads or crack alloy rings.
* Front derailleur mount bolt: 5 to 7 Nm. Keeps the derailleur at the correct height and angle over the chainrings.
* Rear derailleur mount bolt (hanger): 8 to 10 Nm. A loose hanger lets the derailleur shift, so shifting becomes poor. The hanger can bend if it moves in a crash.
* Derailleur cable pinch bolt: 4 to 5 Nm. Clamps the cable. Too tight can crush the cable and make shifting stiff.

### Accessories

* Water bottle cage bolts: follow the frame spec, often a low value. Carbon frames use less torque than steel or aluminum frames because the bosses can crack.
* Rack and fender bolts: about 5 Nm for most aluminum and steel mounts. Loose bolts rattle and can cause the rack to shift.

* Bolts that were torqued, then loosened, and then retightened should be checked against the spec again.
* A torque wrench is a precision tool. Store it at its lowest setting and check it periodically against a known reference if you use it often.
* Confirm each value against the component's printed spec before you use it. Manufacturers update their specs, and the values above are general ranges, not exact specs for every product.

# Brake Check Procedure for New Volunteers

Fern Hollow Bicycle Cooperative

Read this whole page before you touch a brake. If you are unsure about any step, stop and ask a shop lead.

## Before you start

You need: 4 mm and 5 mm hex keys, a flat screwdriver, a cone wrench or 15 mm wrench, and a clean rag.

Secure the bike in a stand or turn it upside down on a clean surface. Check that the wheel is seated fully in the dropouts and the quick release or thru axle is closed and tight.

If any step below fails, tag the bike DO NOT RIDE and tell a shop lead before you go on.

## Part 1: Checks for every bike

1. Spin each wheel by hand. It should turn freely and stop slowly. Watch for rubbing on the brake pads, the frame, or the fork. Check that the wheel is centered between the pads or caliper.
2. Squeeze each brake lever firmly. The lever should feel firm, not spongy. It should stop well before it touches the handlebar.
3. Look at the cables or hoses. Cables should not be frayed, kinked, or rusty. Cable housing ends should be intact. Hydraulic hoses should have no cracks, bulges, or wet spots.
4. Check the brake pads. Replace a pad when its grooves are gone or the rubber is thinner than about 1.5 mm. Pads should not be cracked, glazed (shiny and hard), or oily.
5. Check the brake lever bolt and clamp. The lever should not slip or rotate on the bar.

## Part 2: Rim brakes

Rim brakes squeeze the sides of the wheel rim.

**Pad position**
- Each pad should land on the smooth braking track of the rim, not on the tire or the rim edge.
- Pads should sit about 1 mm to 2 mm from the rim when the lever is released.
- Both pads should touch the rim at the same time when you squeeze the lever. Center them if one touches first.
- Toe in each pad slightly so the front edge touches the rim about 1 mm before the back edge. This stops squeal.

**Pad bolts and cables**
- Pad bolts and the cable pinch bolt should be snug and not loose.
- Use the barrel adjuster on the lever or caliper to fine tune cable tension. If the adjuster is at its limit, the cable needs a lead to fix.

**Rim wear**
- Look at the braking track. If it has deep grooves, a dip, a bulge, or a wear indicator that shows through, tag the wheel and tell a lead. Do not keep riding on a worn rim.

**Test**
- Squeeze the front lever. Both pads should grab the rim evenly.
- Spin the wheel. It should stop quickly and quietly.
- Repeat for the rear.

## Part 3: Disc brakes

Disc brakes squeeze a rotor bolted to the hub. There are mechanical (cable) and hydraulic (fluid) types.

**Rotor**
- Look for cracks, bends, or deep scoring. Spin the wheel and watch for rubbing.
- Check the rotor bolts are snug. Use the torque value printed on the rotor or caliper if you have a torque wrench.
- Rotors must be free of oil. If a rotor has oil or grease on it, tag the bike and tell a lead.

**Caliper**
- Check the caliper mount bolts are tight.
- The caliper should sit centered over the rotor with no rubbing on either side.
- To center a caliper: loosen the mount bolts slightly, squeeze and hold the lever, then tighten the bolts with the lever still held.

**Pads**
- Replace a pad when the wear groove is gone or the friction material is thinner than about 0.5 mm.
- Pads should not be glazed, cracked, or oily.

**Mechanical disc (cable)**
- Use the barrel adjuster to set the pad clearance. Brakes should engage with a short lever pull and no rub when released.
- If the cable is frayed, sticky, or the adjuster has run out, tell a lead.

**Hydraulic disc**
- Look for leaks at the lever, the caliper, and the hose joints. Any leak or wet fluid means DO NOT RIDE.
- The lever should feel firm and consistent. If the lever feels spongy or pulls to the bar, DO NOT RIDE and tell a lead. Do not open the fluid system or bleed brakes unless a trained lead asks you to.

**Test**
- Squeeze the lever. The wheel should stop fast with steady lever feel.
- Release the lever. The wheel should spin with no rub.
- Test the front and rear brakes separately.

## Stop and tag the bike if you see any of these

- Cracked lever, lever body, or caliper
- Frayed, kinked, or rusty cable, or a cracked housing end
- Hydraulic leak, bulge, or spongy lever
- Bent or cracked rotor, or oil on the rotor
- Pads below the limits above, or pads that are glazed or oily
- Rim worn through the braking track, or a bulge on the rim
- A brake that does not stop the wheel
- Any brake you are not sure about

Tag the bike DO NOT RIDE, write what you saw on the tag, and tell a shop lead.

## When you finish

Record which brakes you checked, what you adjusted, and what parts you replaced. Give the bike to a lead for sign off before it goes back to a member.

## Part 1: Checks for every bike

1. Spin each wheel by hand. It should turn freely and stop slowly. Watch for rubbing on the brake pads, the frame, or the fork. Check that the wheel is centered between the pads or caliper.
2. Squeeze each brake lever firmly. The lever should feel firm, not spongy. It should stop well before it touches the handlebar.
3. Look at the cables or hoses. Cables should not be frayed, kinked, or rusty. Cable housing ends should be intact. Hydraulic hoses should have no cracks, bulges, or wet spots.
4. Check the brake pads. Replace a pad when its grooves are gone or the rubber is thinner than about 1.5 mm. Pads should not be cracked, glazed (shiny and hard), or oily.
5. Check the brake lever bolt and clamp. The lever should not slip or rotate on the bar.

## Part 2: Rim brakes

Rim brakes squeeze the sides of the wheel rim.

**Pad position**
- Each pad should land on the smooth braking track of the rim, not on the tire or the rim edge.
- Pads should sit about 1 mm to 2 mm from the rim when the lever is released.
- Both pads should touch the rim at the same time when you squeeze the lever. Center them if one touches first.
- Toe in each pad slightly so the front edge touches the rim about 1 mm before the back edge. This stops squeal.

**Pad bolts and cables**
- Pad bolts and the cable pinch bolt should be snug and not loose.
- Use the barrel adjuster on the lever or caliper to fine tune cable tension. If the adjuster is at its limit, the cable needs a lead to fix.

**Rim wear**
- Look at the braking track. If it has deep grooves, a dip, a bulge, or a wear indicator that shows through, tag the wheel and tell a lead. Do not keep riding on a worn rim.

**Test**
- Squeeze the front lever. Both pads should grab the rim evenly.
- Spin the wheel. It should stop quickly and quietly.
- Repeat for the rear.

## Part 3: Disc brakes

Disc brakes squeeze a rotor bolted to the hub. There are mechanical (cable) and hydraulic (fluid) types.

**Rotor**
- Look for cracks, bends, or deep scoring. Spin the wheel and watch for rubbing.
- Check the rotor bolts are snug. Use the torque value printed on the rotor or caliper if you have a torque wrench.
- Rotors must be free of oil. If a rotor has oil or grease on it, tag the bike and tell a lead.

**Caliper**
- Check the caliper mount bolts are tight.
- The caliper should sit centered over the rotor with no rubbing on either side.
- To center a caliper: loosen the mount bolts slightly, squeeze and hold the lever, then tighten the bolts with the lever still held.

**Pads**
- Replace a pad when the wear groove is gone or the friction material is thinner than about 0.5 mm.
- Pads should not be glazed, cracked, or oily.

**Mechanical disc (cable)**
- Use the barrel adjuster to set the pad clearance. Brakes should engage with a short lever pull and no rub when released.
- If the cable is frayed, sticky, or the adjuster has run out, tell a lead.

**Hydraulic disc**
- Look for leaks at the lever, the caliper, and the hose joints. Any leak or wet fluid means DO NOT RIDE.
- The lever should feel firm and consistent. If the lever feels spongy or pulls to the bar, DO NOT RIDE and tell a lead. Do not open the fluid system or bleed brakes unless a trained lead asks you to.

**Test**
- Squeeze the lever. The wheel should stop fast with steady lever feel.
- Release the lever. The wheel should spin with no rub.
- Test the front and rear brakes separately.

## Stop and tag the bike if you see any of these

- Cracked lever, lever body, or caliper
- Frayed, kinked, or rusty cable, or a cracked housing end
- Hydraulic leak, bulge, or spongy lever
- Bent or cracked rotor, or oil on the rotor
- Pads below the limits above, or pads that are glazed or oily
- Rim worn through the braking track, or a bulge on the rim
- A brake that does not stop the wheel
- Any brake you are not sure about

Tag the bike DO NOT RIDE, write what you saw on the tag, and tell a shop lead.

## When you finish

Record which brakes you checked, what you adjusted, and what parts you replaced. Give the bike to a lead for sign off before it goes back to a member.

# Bike Torque Reference

Torque wrenches measure how hard a fastener is tightened. Bike parts are thin, light, and often made of aluminum or carbon fiber. Too little torque lets a part loosen or slip. Too much torque can crack carbon, strip threads, crush a bearing, or warp a clamp. A torque wrench lets you hit the window the manufacturer specifies, which is usually a narrow range.

Torque is measured in newton meters (Nm). Some older tools and manuals use inch pounds (in lb). To convert, multiply Nm by 8.85 to get in lb.

## Why torque matters on a bike

- Clamps hold by friction. Too little torque means the stem, seatpost, or bar can slip under load. Too much can crush carbon or deform aluminum.
- Threads can strip or gall, especially in aluminum frames and alloy bolts.
- Carbon parts can crack without warning when overtightened.
- Brake and rotor bolts must be tight enough to avoid rattling or shifting under braking.
- Crank and pedal threads need high, steady torque so they do not loosen while pedaling.

## Typical values

These are common ranges for most road and mountain bikes. Always check the marking on the part or the manufacturer manual first. The number printed on a stem, seatpost, or frame governs over this table.

| Fastener | Typical torque | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Stem faceplate bolts (to bar) | 5 to 6 Nm | Clamps the bar. Carbon bars often specify lower values. |
| Steerer expander bolt (stem top plug) | 4 to 6 Nm | Expands the steerer to hold the stem. Too much can crack a carbon steerer. |
| Headset top cap bolt | 3 to 5 Nm | Sets bearing preload. Tighten only until the bars stop moving on the front wheel lock. Overtightening damages bearings. |
| Seatpost clamp bolt | 5 to 7 Nm | Holds the post in the frame. Carbon posts often need a specific value. |
| Saddle rail clamp bolts | 5 to 7 Nm | Holds the saddle rails. Overtightening can crack carbon rails. |
| Brake lever clamp bolt | 1 to 2 Nm | Keeps the lever from rotating on the bar. Very light torque. |
| Shifter clamp bolt | 2 to 3 Nm | Holds the shifter on the bar. Overtightening can crack carbon bars. |
| Rim brake caliper mounting bolt | 6 to 8 Nm | Holds the caliper to the frame or fork so the pads track correctly. |
| Disc brake caliper mounting bolts | 6 to 8 Nm | Holds the caliper to the mount. Too loose causes rubbing or shifting. |
| Disc rotor bolts (6 bolt) | 2 to 4 Nm | Holds the rotor to the hub. Low torque prevents warping the rotor. |
| Centerlock rotor lockring | 40 Nm | Clamps the rotor. Check the hub maker value, which is often 40 Nm. |
| Front thru axle | 10 to 15 Nm | Clamps the fork dropouts. Check the axle and fork spec. |
| Rear thru axle | 10 to 15 Nm | Clamps the rear triangle. Check the axle spec. |
| Crank arm bolt (self extracting or Hollowtech style) | 35 to 50 Nm | Holds the crank to the spindle. Too loose causes creaking and damage. |
| Bottom bracket cups or lockring | 35 to 55 Nm | Holds the bottom bracket in the frame. Check frame and BB maker spec. |
| Pedals (into crank) | 30 to 35 Nm | Holds the pedal in the crank. Right pedal uses normal thread. Left pedal uses reverse thread. |
| Cassette lockring | 30 to 40 Nm | Holds the cassette cogs on the freehub. |
| Chainring bolts | 8 to 12 Nm | Holds the rings to the crank spider. Torque in a star pattern. |
| Front derailleur clamp bolt | 5 to 7 Nm | Holds the derailleur on the seat tube. Too loose lets it shift. |
| Rear derailleur mounting bolt | 8 to 10 Nm | Holds the derailleur to the hanger. Overtightening can bend or break the hanger. |
| Bottle cage bolts | 4 to 5 Nm | Holds the cage to the frame. Overtightening can crack carbon frames. |
| Rack or fender bolts | 4 to 5 Nm | Holds accessories. Light torque protects threads. |

## Using the table

1. Read the spec on the part first. Frame, stem, seatpost, and crank markings take priority over this table.
2. Clean and lightly grease threads only where the manufacturer allows. Grease changes the friction, so the same torque can clamp harder. Some carbon parts require dry threads.
3. Tighten in a cross or star pattern on multi bolt parts, such as chainrings and rotors.
4. Set the wrench to the value, then pull smoothly until it clicks or beeps. Do not keep pulling after the click.
5. Recheck clamp bolts after the first few rides.

## Notes

- These values are typical ranges. They are not a substitute for manufacturer specs.
- A clicker wrench must be calibrated and stored at its lowest setting.
- Torque wrenches are precision tools. Drop them and they may read wrong.

| Disc brake caliper mounting bolts | 6 to 8 Nm | Holds the caliper to the mount. Too loose causes rubbing or shifting. |
| Disc rotor bolts (6 bolt) | 2 to 4 Nm | Holds the rotor to the hub. Low torque prevents warping the rotor. |
| Centerlock rotor lockring | 40 Nm | Clamps the rotor. Check the hub maker value, which is often 40 Nm. |
| Front thru axle | 10 to 15 Nm | Clamps the fork dropouts. Check the axle and fork spec. |
| Rear thru axle | 10 to 15 Nm | Clamps the rear triangle. Check the axle spec. |
| Crank arm bolt (self extracting or Hollowtech style) | 35 to 50 Nm | Holds the crank to the spindle. Too loose causes creaking and damage. |
| Bottom bracket cups or lockring | 35 to 55 Nm | Holds the bottom bracket in the frame. Check frame and BB maker spec. |
| Pedals (into crank) | 30 to 35 Nm | Holds the pedal in the crank. Right pedal uses normal thread. Left pedal uses reverse thread. |
| Cassette lockring | 30 to 40 Nm | Holds the cassette cogs on the freehub. |
| Chainring bolts | 8 to 12 Nm | Holds the rings to the crank spider. Torque in a star pattern. |
| Front derailleur clamp bolt | 5 to 7 Nm | Holds the derailleur on the seat tube. Too loose lets it shift. |
| Rear derailleur mounting bolt | 8 to 10 Nm | Holds the derailleur to the hanger. Overtightening can bend or break the hanger. |
| Bottle cage bolts | 4 to 5 Nm | Holds the cage to the frame. Overtightening can crack carbon frames. |
| Rack or fender bolts | 4 to 5 Nm | Holds accessories. Light torque protects threads. |

## Using the table

1. Read the spec on the part first. Frame, stem, seatpost, and crank markings take priority over this table.
2. Clean and lightly grease threads only where the manufacturer allows. Grease changes the friction, so the same torque can clamp harder. Some carbon parts require dry threads.
3. Tighten in a cross or star pattern on multi bolt parts, such as chainrings and rotors.
4. Set the wrench to the value, then pull smoothly until it clicks or beeps. Do not keep pulling after the click.
5. Recheck clamp bolts after the first few rides.

## Notes

- These values are typical ranges. They are not a substitute for manufacturer specs.
- A clicker wrench must be calibrated and stored at its lowest setting.
- Torque wrenches are precision tools. Drop them and they may read wrong.

# Chain and Cassette Wear

## Why chains wear out

A bike chain is a row of small steel pins and rollers. Each link pivots on a pin inside a bushing. Every pedal stroke moves those parts against each other, and grit that gets past the lube grinds the pins and plates. Over time the pin wears, the pitch (the distance from one pin to the next) grows, and the chain gets longer. The chain does not stretch like rubber. The metal wears where the parts meet.

A worn chain has two problems. First, it no longer meshes cleanly with the cassette teeth. Second, a longer chain wears the cassette faster, because each link lands on a different tooth position and pushes the cassette teeth into a hooked shape.

Clean and lube reduce wear. Riding in wet or gritty conditions, or using too much lube that picks up dirt, speeds it up.

## How to measure wear

Use a chain wear indicator tool, such as a Park Tool CC-2 or similar. Hook the tool onto the chain and check the reading. Measure with the chain under light tension, on a clean chain, at several spots around the loop.

If you do not have a tool, measure by hand:

1. Choose a point on the chain. Measure exactly 12 inches from the outside edge of one pin to the outside edge of the pin 12 inches along. A standard chain has 24 links over 12 inches.
2. Compare the length to 12 inches.
3. Calculate the wear percentage: (measured length minus 12) divided by 12, times 100.

Typical replacement thresholds:

- About 0.5 percent elongation for 11 and 12 speed chains. That is about 0.06 inches over 12 inches.
- About 0.75 percent elongation for 10 speed and older chains. That is about 0.09 inches over 12 inches.
- Check the manufacturer's spec for your chain, because some are rated differently.

## When to replace the chain

Replace the chain when it reaches the thresholds above. Check at several points, because a chain can wear unevenly. Replace it before the cassette wears, because a new cassette costs more than a chain.

A chain that has worn past the threshold will skip under load, especially on the largest rear cogs, and will make the cassette wear faster. Check the chain every few hundred miles, or more often in wet or dusty conditions.

## When to replace the cassette

The cassette is worn when its teeth have changed shape. Look at the teeth on the largest cogs and the cogs you use most:

- Teeth are hooked, shark fin shaped, or pointed instead of flat on the front edge.
- Teeth are visibly thinner or narrower than new teeth.
- The chain skips or jumps under pedaling load, but not when it is off the bike or lightly loaded.

If the cassette is worn, a new chain will also skip on it. Replacing only the cassette with a worn chain leads to fast wear on the new cassette, so replace the chain at the same time.

A worn cassette does not always need to be replaced at the same time as the chain. Replace the cassette when it shows the wear signs above and the new chain still skips on it.

## Summary

1. Chains wear because metal pins and bushings grind against each other, and grit speeds this up.
2. Measure with a chain wear tool, or with a 12 inch ruler over 24 links.
3. Replace the chain at about 0.5 percent for 11 and 12 speed, and about 0.75 percent for 10 speed and older.
4. Replace the cassette when its teeth are hooked or thin, or when a new chain skips on it.
5. Replace the chain before the cassette to protect the cassette.
